facts.fact: In the 2023 NEC, almost all definitions that used to sit in the .2 section of individual articles were moved into Article 100, which now holds roughly 800 definitions in one alphabetical list. In NEC 2020 many definitions were still found inside their own articles.
A continuous load is one where the maximum current is expected to continue for 3 hours or more.

Readily accessible means it can be reached quickly for operation, renewal or inspection without having to use tools (other than keys), climb over or under things, remove obstacles, or use a portable ladder.
Ampacity is the maximum current, in amperes, that a conductor can carry continuously under its conditions of use without exceeding its temperature rating.
A branch circuit is the circuit conductors between the final overcurrent device protecting the circuit and the outlet(s).
A feeder is all circuit conductors between the service equipment (or the source of a separately derived system or other power supply) and the final branch-circuit overcurrent device.

A multiwire branch circuit has two or more ungrounded conductors with voltage between them and a grounded (neutral) conductor that has equal voltage to each ungrounded conductor, such as a 120/240 V shared-neutral circuit.

facts.source: NEC 2023 Article 100 (Grounded Conductor; Equipment Grounding Conductor)
facts.fact: The grounded conductor is the circuit conductor that is intentionally grounded (usually the white or gray neutral). The equipment grounding conductor (EGC) is the path that connects normally non-current-carrying metal parts of equipment together and to the system grounded conductor and/or grounding electrode conductor (green or bare).
The grounding electrode conductor (GEC) is the conductor that connects the system grounded conductor or the equipment to a grounding electrode or to a point on the grounding electrode system.

facts.source: NEC 2023 Article 100 (Bonding Jumper, Main; Bonding Jumper, System)
facts.fact: The main bonding jumper connects the grounded (neutral) conductor to the equipment grounding conductor and/or supply-side bonding jumper at the service. A system bonding jumper makes that same connection at a separately derived system such as a transformer.

facts.source: NEC 2023 Article 100 (Service Point; Service Drop; Service Lateral)
facts.fact: The service point is where the serving utility's facilities connect to the premises wiring. A service drop is the overhead utility conductors to the service point, and a service lateral is the underground utility conductors to the service point.
A dwelling unit is a single unit providing complete and independent living facilities for one or more persons, with permanent provisions for living, sleeping, cooking and sanitation.
'In sight from' (within sight) means the equipment is visible from the other equipment and not more than 50 ft away.

Listed equipment appears in a list published by an organization acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction (for example UL) showing it meets standards or was tested and found suitable. Labeled equipment carries that organization's label, symbol or identifying mark.

A damp location is protected from weather but subject to moderate moisture, such as under canopies or roofed open porches. A wet location is underground, in concrete slabs or masonry in direct contact with the earth, subject to saturation, or unprotected and exposed to weather.

A qualified person has skills and knowledge related to the construction and operation of the electrical equipment and installations and has received safety training to recognize and avoid the hazards involved.

Overcurrent is any current above the rating of equipment or the ampacity of a conductor, caused by overload, short circuit or ground fault. An overload is operation above normal full-load rating that causes damage if it lasts long enough; a short circuit or ground fault is not an overload.
A GFCI protects people by de-energizing a circuit when ground-fault current exceeds Class A values. A Class A GFCI trips when ground-fault current is 6 mA or higher and does not trip below 4 mA.
Mandatory NEC rules use 'shall' or 'shall not'. Permissive rules use 'shall be permitted' or 'shall not be required'. Informational notes are explanatory only and are not enforceable requirements.

The NEC's purpose is practical safeguarding of people and property from electrical hazards. It is not a design specification or an instruction manual for untrained persons, and compliance gives an essentially hazard-free but not necessarily efficient or expandable installation.

A separately derived system is an electrical source other than a service that has no direct connection to the circuit conductors of another source except through grounding and bonding connections. A typical example is the secondary of a dry-type transformer.
A raceway is an enclosed channel designed expressly to hold wires, cables or busbars, such as EMT, RMC or PVC conduit. A cable tray is a support system, not a raceway.

An outlet is a point on the wiring system where current is taken to supply utilization equipment. A receptacle is a contact device installed at an outlet; a duplex receptacle is two receptacles on one yoke.
A building is a structure that stands alone or that is separated from adjoining structures by fire walls.
Listed or labeled equipment must be installed and used according to any instructions included in the listing or labeling.
Electrical equipment must be installed in a neat and workmanlike manner, and unused openings in boxes, raceways and enclosures must be closed with protection equivalent to the wall of the equipment.

Terminations for circuits rated 100 A or less, or marked for 14 AWG through 1 AWG conductors, are based on 60 C conductor ampacity unless the equipment is listed and marked for 75 C, in which case the 75 C ampacity may be used.
Terminations for circuits rated over 100 A, or marked for conductors larger than 1 AWG, are based on the 75 C ampacity of the conductor.

Equipment intended to interrupt current at fault levels (breakers, fuses) must have an interrupting rating at nominal circuit voltage at least equal to the fault current available at its line terminals.

Service equipment in other than dwelling units must be field marked with the maximum available fault current and the date the calculation was done, and the marking must be updated when changes alter the available fault current.

In other than dwelling units, equipment such as switchboards, switchgear, enclosed panelboards, industrial control panels, meter socket enclosures and motor control centers that may be examined, adjusted, serviced or maintained while energized must be marked to warn of arc-flash hazards.

Under NEC 2023, in other than dwelling units, service equipment and feeder-supplied equipment rated 1000 A or more needs a permanent arc-flash label that follows industry practice and includes the date it was applied. NEC 2020 applied this only to service equipment rated 1200 A or more and required nominal voltage, available fault current, clearing time and date.

Working space in front of electrical equipment must be at least 30 in wide or the width of the equipment, whichever is greater, and equipment doors or hinged panels must be able to open at least 90 degrees.
For 151-600 V to ground (such as 480Y/277 V), minimum working space depth is 3 ft for Condition 1, 3-1/2 ft for Condition 2, and 4 ft for Condition 3.
For 601-1000 V to ground, minimum working space depth is 3 ft for Condition 1, 4 ft for Condition 2, and 5 ft for Condition 3.

Condition 1: exposed live parts on one side and no live or grounded parts on the other (or effectively guarded by insulation). Condition 2: exposed live parts on one side and grounded parts on the other; concrete, brick or tile walls count as grounded. Condition 3: exposed live parts on both sides.

Indoor switchboards, panelboards and similar equipment get a dedicated electrical space equal to the equipment's width and depth, from the floor to 6 ft above the equipment or to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower. No piping, ducts or other foreign systems may be installed in that zone.

For equipment rated 1200 A or more and over 6 ft wide that contains overcurrent, switching or control devices, there must be an entrance at each end of the working space at least 24 in wide and 6-1/2 ft high (with exceptions for an unobstructed exit or doubled working space).

Where equipment rated 800 A or more contains overcurrent, switching or control devices, personnel doors within 25 ft of the nearest edge of the working space must open in the direction of egress and have listed panic or fire exit hardware.

Illumination must be provided for working spaces about service equipment, switchboards, switchgear, panelboards and motor control centers installed indoors, and it may not be controlled only by automatic means.

Working space height is 6-1/2 ft or the equipment height, whichever is greater, and other equipment above or below (such as wireways) may extend no more than 6 in beyond the front of the electrical equipment.

Live parts operating at 50 V or more must be guarded against accidental contact by an enclosure, a room accessible only to qualified persons, permanent partitions or screens, or elevation of at least 8 ft above the floor.

On a 4-wire delta system where the midpoint of one phase winding is grounded, the phase with the higher voltage to ground (the high leg) must be durably marked orange or by another effective means wherever the neutral is also present.
Field-applied hazard warning labels must use effective words, colors and/or symbols, be permanently affixed, and may not be handwritten (except for portions that are variable).
New in NEC 2023, the floor, grade or platform within the required working space must be kept clear and as level and flat as practical for the full depth and width of the space.

A grounded (neutral) conductor 6 AWG or smaller must be identified by a continuous white or gray outer finish, or by three continuous white or gray stripes along its entire length on insulation that is not green.
A grounded conductor 4 AWG or larger may be identified at the time of installation by a distinctive white or gray marking (such as tape) at its terminations, encircling the conductor.

An equipment grounding conductor may be bare, covered or insulated; if insulated it must be green or green with one or more yellow stripes. Conductors larger than 6 AWG may be reidentified as an EGC at each end and accessible point by stripping, green coloring or green tape.

A white or gray conductor in a cable may be used as an ungrounded (hot) conductor, such as in a switch loop, only if it is permanently reidentified (tape, paint, etc.) at every location where it is visible and accessible. In a switch loop it may be used only to supply the switch, not as the return.

Each multiwire branch circuit must have a means at its point of origin that simultaneously disconnects all of its ungrounded conductors, such as a 2-pole breaker or single-pole breakers with identified handle ties.
The ungrounded and grounded conductors of each multiwire branch circuit must be grouped together (for example with cable ties) in at least one location within the panelboard or other point of origin.

In a multiwire branch circuit, the continuity of the grounded (neutral) conductor may not depend on device connections such as receptacle terminals; neutrals must be spliced (pigtailed) so removing a device does not open the neutral.

Informational notes recommend sizing branch-circuit conductors for no more than 3% voltage drop at the farthest outlet, and no more than 5% total voltage drop on feeder plus branch circuit. These notes are recommendations, not enforceable rules.
A single receptacle installed on an individual branch circuit must have an ampere rating not less than that of the branch circuit.
Receptacle ratings permitted on multi-outlet circuits: 15 A circuit, 15 A receptacles only; 20 A circuit, 15 A or 20 A receptacles; 30 A circuit, 30 A; 40 A circuit, 40 A or 50 A; 50 A circuit, 50 A.
Maximum cord-and-plug load on a receptacle: a 15 A receptacle on a 15 A or 20 A circuit, 12 A; a 20 A receptacle on a 20 A circuit, 16 A; a 30 A receptacle on a 30 A circuit, 24 A (80% of rating).

On a 15 A or 20 A branch circuit, one cord-and-plug-connected piece of equipment not fastened in place may not exceed 80% of the circuit rating, and equipment fastened in place (other than luminaires) may not exceed 50% of the rating when lighting or cord-connected equipment is also supplied.
facts.note: NEC 2023 renumbered: the new 10 A circuit rules took 210.23(A), so 15/20 A rules are 210.23(B).

facts.fact: New in NEC 2023, 10 A branch circuits may supply only lighting outlets, dwelling exhaust fans on bathroom or laundry lighting circuits, or a gas fireplace on an individual circuit. They may not supply receptacle outlets, fixed appliances, garage door openers or laundry equipment, and use at least 14 AWG copper (12 AWG aluminum). NEC 2020 had no 10 A branch circuit rating.

NEC 2023 added 10 A to the list of standard overcurrent device ratings (so 10 A circuit breakers are standard). In NEC 2020 the list began at 15 A, and 10 A appeared only among the additional standard fuse ratings.
Branch-circuit conductors for a household range rated 8-3/4 kW or more must have a rating of at least 40 A.
Tap conductors from a 50 A range branch circuit to a wall-mounted oven or counter-mounted cooking unit must have an ampacity of at least 20 A and be no longer than needed for servicing.
A dwelling must have at least one additional 20 A branch circuit to supply the laundry receptacle outlet(s), and that circuit may have no other outlets.

A dwelling needs at least one 120 V, 20 A branch circuit for bathroom receptacles. That circuit may serve receptacles in more than one bathroom but no other outlets, or it may serve all the outlets (lighting, fan) in a single bathroom.

A dwelling needs at least one 120 V, 20 A branch circuit for receptacle outlets in an attached garage, and in a detached garage that has power. (Required since NEC 2020; NEC 2023 clarifies that additional garage circuits are allowed.)

Dwelling small-appliance branch circuits serve receptacles in the kitchen, pantry, breakfast room, dining room and similar areas and may have no other outlets, except a clock receptacle or supplemental equipment/lighting on gas ranges. A refrigerator may instead be on its own individual branch circuit rated 15 A or more.
In dwelling units, the voltage between conductors supplying luminaires and cord-and-plug loads of 1440 VA or less (or less than 1/4 hp) may not exceed 120 V.

For dwelling receptacle spacing, a wall space is any wall 2 ft or more wide, measured around corners and unbroken by doorways, fireplaces and similar openings; fixed panels of exterior walls and fixed room dividers such as bar-type counters and railings also count.
A floor receptacle counts toward the required wall receptacles only if it is within 18 in of the wall.

Receptacles that are part of a luminaire or appliance, located inside cabinets or cupboards, controlled by a wall switch used as the room lighting outlet, or located more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor do not count as required dwelling receptacles.
Every kitchen countertop or work-surface wall space 12 in or wider must have a receptacle outlet.
Kitchen countertop receptacles must be on or above the countertop, not more than 20 in above it, or in the countertop using listed countertop receptacle assemblies.

Under NEC 2020, an island or peninsula countertop needed at least one receptacle for the first 9 sq ft (or fraction) and one more for every additional 18 sq ft (or fraction). Peninsulas are measured from the connected perpendicular wall, and at least one receptacle must be within 2 ft of the peninsula's outer end.

Under NEC 2023, a receptacle is no longer required on a kitchen island or peninsula; if none is installed, provisions for adding one later (such as a raceway or cable to a covered box) must be provided. Receptacles below the countertop (allowed up to 12 in below in NEC 2020) are no longer permitted.

At least one bathroom receptacle must be within 3 ft of the outside edge of each basin, on an adjacent wall or partition, on the countertop, or on the side or face of the basin cabinet, and never more than 12 in below the top of the basin or countertop.

A one-family dwelling and each unit of a two-family dwelling at grade level must have at least one receptacle at the front and one at the back, readily accessible from grade and not more than 6-1/2 ft above grade.
Balconies, decks and porches accessible from inside a dwelling unit must have at least one receptacle within their perimeter, not more than 6-1/2 ft above the walking surface.
Dwelling garages must have at least one receptacle outlet in each vehicle bay, not more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor.
Each separate unfinished portion of a dwelling basement must have at least one receptacle outlet.
Dwelling hallways 10 ft or more long need at least one receptacle; hall length is measured along the centerline without passing through a doorway.
Dwelling foyers that are not part of a hallway and are larger than 60 sq ft need a receptacle in each wall space 3 ft or more wide.
At least one receptacle outlet must be installed in each dwelling area designated for laundry equipment.

A 125 V, 15 A or 20 A receptacle must be installed at an accessible location within 25 ft of heating, air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment, on the same level, and not connected to the load side of the equipment's disconnect.

NEC 2023 requires, in other than one- and two-family dwellings, a 125 V, 15/20 A receptacle within 25 ft of indoor service equipment and of indoor equipment needing dedicated space. NEC 2020 210.64 required one within 50 ft of the electrical service equipment.
facts.note: 25 ft confirmed from a Mike Holt 2023 summary; the one-/two-family dwelling exclusion and exact (B)(1)/(B)(2) wording were not confirmed against the code text.

facts.fact: NEC 2023 requires at least one receptacle within 18 in of the top of each show window with no point along the top more than 6 ft from a receptacle. NEC 2020 required one receptacle for each 12 linear ft (or major fraction) of show window.

Meeting rooms with any floor dimension of 12 ft or more and at least 215 sq ft need at least one floor receptacle (or floor outlet) at least 6 ft from any fixed wall for each 215 sq ft or major portion.

At least one wall-switch-controlled lighting outlet is required in every habitable room, kitchen and bathroom of a dwelling; in habitable rooms other than kitchens and bathrooms, a switched receptacle may substitute.
Where a dwelling stairway has six or more risers between floor levels, a wall switch for the stairway lighting is required at each floor level and at each landing level that includes an entryway.

Attics, underfloor spaces, utility rooms and basements used for storage or containing equipment requiring servicing need at least one lighting outlet with a switch at the point of entry, with the light at or near the equipment.

Tamper-resistant receptacles are required for 15 A and 20 A, 125 V and 250 V nonlocking receptacles in dwelling units (including garages and accessory buildings), hotel guest rooms, child care facilities, schools, dormitories and similar occupancies; NEC 2023 added more occupancies such as nursing homes and fitness centers.

Tamper-resistant receptacles are not required when located more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor, when part of a luminaire or appliance, for a single or duplex receptacle serving appliances in a dedicated space that are not easily moved, or for nongrounding replacement receptacles.

15 A and 20 A, 125-250 V receptacles in wet locations must have an enclosure that is weatherproof whether or not a plug is inserted (extra-duty 'in-use' cover), and the receptacles must be listed weather-resistant type.

Receptacles may not be installed within a zone 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of a bathtub rim or shower threshold (NEC 2020). NEC 2023 adds that the zone includes the space below it but excludes spaces separated by a floor, wall, ceiling, door, window or fixed barrier.

Where no equipment ground exists, a nongrounding receptacle may be replaced with another nongrounding receptacle, with a GFCI receptacle marked 'No Equipment Ground', or with a grounding-type receptacle protected by a GFCI and marked 'GFCI Protected' and 'No Equipment Ground'.

When replacing a receptacle in a location that now requires GFCI protection, the replacement must be GFCI protected; when replacing one in an area that now requires AFCI protection, the replacement must be AFCI protected.
Receptacles may not be installed face-up in countertops or similar work surfaces unless they are receptacle assemblies listed for countertop applications.

For GFCI distance rules, distance is measured as the shortest path a cord would follow without piercing a floor, wall, ceiling or fixed barrier. NEC 2023 dropped the earlier wording about passing through a door, doorway or window.

Dwelling GFCI protection applies to all 125 V through 250 V receptacles supplied by single-phase branch circuits rated 150 V or less to ground in the listed locations (this 125-250 V scope began in NEC 2020).

NEC 2020 required dwelling kitchen GFCI only for receptacles serving countertop surfaces. NEC 2023 requires GFCI for all receptacles in dwelling kitchens, including refrigerator and range receptacles.
NEC 2023 added GFCI for dwelling receptacles in areas with a sink and permanent provisions for food preparation, beverage preparation or cooking (such as wet bars).
Dwelling receptacles within 6 ft of the top inside edge of a sink bowl, or within 6 ft of the outside edge of a bathtub or shower stall, need GFCI protection.
Dwelling GFCI locations also include garages and accessory buildings, outdoors, crawl spaces at or below grade, basements (finished or unfinished), boathouses and laundry areas.
NEC 2023 added indoor damp and wet locations to the list of dwelling locations requiring GFCI protection for receptacles.

Other-than-dwelling GFCI applies to 125-250 V receptacles on single-phase circuits rated 150 V or less to ground and 50 A or less, and on three-phase circuits rated 150 V or less to ground and 100 A or less.

NEC 2023 commercial GFCI locations include bathrooms, kitchens, food preparation areas, buffet serving areas, rooftops, outdoors, within 6 ft of sinks, indoor damp/wet locations, locker rooms with showers, garages and service bays, crawl spaces, unfinished basements, within 6 ft of aquariums and bait wells, laundry areas, and within 6 ft of bathtubs/showers.

NEC 2023 requires GFCI for the branch circuit or outlet (cord-connected or hardwired) of specific appliances rated 150 V or less to ground and 60 A or less: vending machines, drinking water coolers and bottle fillers, tire inflation and automotive vacuum machines, high-pressure spray washers, sump pumps, dishwashers, electric ranges, wall ovens, counter-mounted cooking units, clothes dryers and microwave ovens.
Under NEC 2020, outlets supplying dishwashers in dwelling units required GFCI protection (210.8(D)); ranges and dryers were not yet on the GFCI list.
GFCI protection is required for the service receptacles required by 210.63 (for example the receptacle within 25 ft of HVAC equipment).

Dwelling outdoor outlets (not just receptacles) supplied by single-phase branch circuits rated 150 V or less to ground and 50 A or less need GFCI protection; NEC 2023 extends this to outlets at garages with floors at or below grade, accessory buildings and boathouses. Lighting outlets are exempt (except crawl space lighting).
TIA 23-3 (effective Sept 1, 2022) added Exception No. 2 exempting listed HVAC equipment from the 210.8(F) outdoor-outlet GFCI rule; that exception was written to expire September 1, 2026.
facts.note: A further TIA proposing extension to Sept 1, 2028 was out for comment in Aug-Sept 2026; check its status and the locally adopted edition.

facts.fact: Lighting outlets not exceeding 120 V in dwelling crawl spaces require GFCI protection.

Dwelling AFCI protection is required for 120 V, single-phase 10 A (new in 2023), 15 A and 20 A branch circuits supplying outlets or devices in kitchens, family rooms, dining rooms, living rooms, parlors, libraries, dens, bedrooms, sunrooms, recreation rooms, closets, hallways, laundry areas and similar areas.
The dwelling AFCI list does not include bathrooms, garages or outdoor outlets, so AFCI is not required there by 210.12 (GFCI rules still apply).
Dormitory units need AFCI protection for 120 V, 10/15/20 A branch circuits supplying outlets in bedrooms, living rooms, hallways, closets, bathrooms and similar rooms.

AFCI protection is also required in hotel and motel guest rooms and suites, patient sleeping rooms in nursing homes and limited-care facilities, and (new in NEC 2023) sleeping quarters of fire, police, ambulance, rescue and ranger stations.

When branch-circuit wiring in an AFCI-required area is modified, replaced or extended, it must be AFCI protected by an AFCI breaker or an outlet branch-circuit AFCI at the first receptacle outlet of the existing circuit. Extensions of 6 ft or less with no added outlets or devices (other than splicing devices) are exempt.

One permitted AFCI method is a listed outlet branch-circuit AFCI at the first outlet with a listed supplemental arc protection breaker, if the home run is no more than 50 ft for 14 AWG or 70 ft for 12 AWG and the first outlet box is marked.

Ground-fault protection of equipment (GFPE) is required for solidly grounded wye services of more than 150 V to ground whose service disconnect is rated 1000 A or more (for example a 480Y/277 V, 1200 A service).
Service GFPE may be set no higher than 1200 A, and the maximum time delay is 1 second for ground-fault currents of 3000 A or more.
A service GFPE system must be performance tested when first installed on site, and a written record of the test must be made available to the authority having jurisdiction.
Feeder disconnects rated 1000 A or more on solidly grounded wye systems over 150 V to ground also need ground-fault protection of equipment, unless GFPE is already provided on the supply side.
In load calculations, fractions of an ampere less than 0.5 may be dropped.
Unless other voltages are specified, load calculations use nominal voltages of 120, 120/240, 208Y/120, 240, 347, 480Y/277, 480, 600Y/347 and 600 V.

Floor area for lighting load is calculated from the outside dimensions of the building. For dwellings, open porches and unfinished spaces not adaptable for future habitable use are excluded. NEC 2023 no longer excludes garages, so garage area is now included; NEC 2020 excluded garages.
The minimum general lighting and general-use receptacle load for dwelling units is 3 VA per sq ft. NEC 2023 moved the dwelling value from Table 220.12 into its own section, 220.41.
In dwelling units, general-use receptacles rated 20 A or less and lighting outlets are already included in the 3 VA/sq ft general lighting load, so no additional 180 VA per receptacle is added.
Non-dwelling general lighting unit loads include office 1.3 VA/sq ft, retail 1.9 VA/sq ft, restaurant 1.5 VA/sq ft and warehouse 1.2 VA/sq ft.

Additional non-dwelling lighting unit loads: schools/universities 1.5, hospitals and health care clinics 1.6, hotels and motels 1.7, manufacturing facilities 2.2, and parking garages 0.3 VA per sq ft.
The 125% continuous-load multiplier is already built into the unit loads in Table 220.42(A) (Table 220.12 in NEC 2020), so it is not applied again to the general lighting load.
Example: a 10,000 sq ft office building has a minimum general lighting load of 10,000 x 1.3 = 13,000 VA.
Dwelling general lighting demand factors: first 3000 VA at 100%, 3001 to 120,000 VA at 35%, and the remainder over 120,000 VA at 25%.

Other lighting demand factors: hospitals, first 50,000 VA at 40% and remainder 20%; hotels/motels without tenant cooking, first 20,000 VA at 50%, 20,001-100,000 at 40%, remainder 30%; warehouses, first 12,500 VA at 100% and remainder 50%; all other occupancies 100%.
Example: a 2,000 sq ft dwelling has 6,000 VA lighting + 3,000 VA (two small-appliance circuits) + 1,500 VA laundry = 10,500 VA. Demand: 3,000 VA at 100% + 7,500 VA x 35% (2,625 VA) = 5,625 VA.

In dwelling load calculations each 20 A small-appliance branch circuit is counted at 1500 VA and the laundry circuit at 1500 VA; these loads may be added to the general lighting load and the lighting demand factors applied.

In non-dwelling occupancies, each single or multiple receptacle on one yoke is calculated at 180 VA; a single piece of equipment made up of four or more receptacles is calculated at 90 VA per receptacle.
Non-dwelling receptacle loads calculated at 180 VA each may be reduced: first 10 kVA at 100% and the remainder over 10 kVA at 50%.

Fixed multioutlet assemblies (plugmold) are calculated at 180 VA per 5 ft (or fraction) where appliances are unlikely to be used at the same time, or 180 VA per 1 ft where they are likely to be used simultaneously.
Show window lighting is calculated at not less than 200 VA per linear foot of show window, measured horizontally along its base.

Each commercial building and occupancy accessible to pedestrians must have at least one sign outlet at each entrance, supplied by a branch circuit rated at least 20 A that supplies no other load, and each required sign circuit is calculated at a minimum of 1200 VA.
In banks and office buildings, the receptacle load is the larger of the calculated receptacle load (180 VA per outlet after demand factors) or 1 VA per sq ft.
Outlets for heavy-duty lampholders are calculated at a minimum of 600 VA each.

In dwellings, four or more appliances fastened in place on the same feeder or service may be calculated at 75% of nameplate. Ranges, clothes dryers, space heating and air conditioning are excluded; NEC 2023 also excludes EVSE and all fastened-in-place household cooking equipment.
Example: a 4,500 W water heater, 1,200 W dishwasher, 900 W disposal and 1,000 W trash compactor total 7,600 W; since there are four appliances, 75% applies: 7,600 x 0.75 = 5,700 VA.
Household clothes dryers are calculated at 5000 W (VA) or the nameplate rating, whichever is larger, per dryer; Table 220.54 demand factors may be applied.
Dryer demand factors: 1-4 dryers 100%, 5 dryers 85%, 6 dryers 75%, 7 dryers 65%, 8 dryers 60%, 9 dryers 55%, 10 dryers 50%, 11 dryers 47%.
For 12-23 dryers the demand factor is 47% minus 1% for each dryer over 11; for 24-42 dryers, 35% minus 0.5% for each dryer over 23; for 43 or more dryers, 25%.
Using Column C, one household range rated not over 12 kW is calculated at a demand of 8 kW.
Column C maximum demand for ranges not over 12 kW: 2 ranges 11 kW, 3 ranges 14 kW, 4 ranges 17 kW, 5 ranges 20 kW.
For ranges over 12 kW through 27 kW of equal rating, Column C is increased 5% for each kW (or major fraction) over 12 kW. Example: one 16 kW range is 4 kW over, so 8 kW x 1.20 = 9.6 kW.

Column A (appliances under 3-1/2 kW) demand: 1 appliance 80%, 2 appliances 75%, 3 appliances 70%, 4 appliances 66%. Column B (3-1/2 to 8-3/4 kW): 1 appliance 80%, 2 appliances 65%, 3 appliances 55%, 4 appliances 50%.

The branch-circuit load for one wall-mounted oven or one counter-mounted cooking unit is its nameplate rating. A counter-mounted cooking unit and up to two wall-mounted ovens in the same room on one branch circuit may be added together and treated as one range.
Example: a 6 kW cooktop and a 4 kW wall oven in the same kitchen on one circuit total 10 kW, treated as one range not over 12 kW, so the demand is 8 kW (Column C).

Commercial kitchen equipment demand factors: 1-2 units 100%, 3 units 90%, 4 units 80%, 5 units 70%, 6 or more units 65%, but the demand may not be less than the sum of the two largest pieces of equipment.
Where loads are unlikely to be used at the same time (such as heating and air conditioning), only the larger load needs to be included in the calculation.
New in NEC 2023, electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) load is calculated at 7200 W (VA) or the nameplate rating, whichever is larger.
Fixed electric space heating loads are calculated at 100% of the total connected load in the standard method.

A feeder or service neutral may be reduced: the first 200 A of unbalanced load at 100% plus the portion over 200 A at 70%. Electric ranges, ovens, cooking units and dryers may be figured at 70% of their demand load for the neutral.
No neutral reduction is permitted for the portion of the load made up of nonlinear loads supplied from a 3-phase, 4-wire wye system.
The dwelling optional calculation applies to a single dwelling unit served by a 120/240 V or 208Y/120 V, 3-wire service or feeder with an ampacity of 100 A or more.

Optional method general loads (3 VA/sq ft, 1500 VA per small-appliance and laundry circuit, nameplate of fixed appliances, ranges, ovens, dryers, water heaters and motors) are taken at 100% of the first 10 kVA plus 40% of the remainder.

Optional method heating/AC: use the largest of 100% of air conditioning; 100% of heat pump compressor plus supplemental heat (unless they cannot run together); 65% of central electric space heat; 65% of space heating with fewer than four separately controlled units; or 40% with four or more separately controlled units.
Example: optional-method general loads of 40 kVA give 10 kVA + 40% x 30 kVA = 22 kVA; adding 5 kVA of air conditioning gives 27 kVA, or 27,000 / 240 V = 112.5 A.
For an existing dwelling where no additional air conditioning or electric space heating is being added, the load may be calculated at 100% of the first 8 kVA plus 40% of the remainder.

The multifamily optional calculation applies to three or more dwelling units, each served by one 3-wire 120/240 V or 208Y/120 V feeder, with electric cooking and electric space heating and/or air conditioning; house loads are calculated separately and added.
Multifamily optional demand factors: 3-5 units 45%, 6-7 units 44%, 8-10 units 43%, 11 units 42%, 12-13 units 41%, 14-15 units 40%, 16-17 units 39%, 18-20 units 38%.
Further multifamily optional demand factors: 21 units 37%, 24-25 units 35%, 28-30 units 33%, 39-42 units 28%, 46-50 units 26%, 56-61 units 24%, 62 and more units 23%.

Existing load may be based on actual maximum demand data for 1 year, or (if not available) the highest 15-minute average demand recorded over at least 30 days; 125% of that maximum demand plus the new load may not exceed the feeder ampacity or service rating.
New in NEC 2023, where an energy management system limits load, the feeder or service calculation may use a single value equal to the system's maximum ampere setpoint.

Overhead service conductors must have at least 8 ft 6 in (2.6 m) vertical clearance above a roof under NEC 2023; NEC 2020 required 8 ft. The clearance is maintained for 3 ft in all directions from the roof edge.
Where the voltage between conductors does not exceed 300 V and the roof slope is at least 4 in. in 12 in., the clearance above the roof may be reduced to 3 ft.

Where the voltage does not exceed 300 V and the conductors pass over only the overhanging portion of the roof (not more than 6 ft of conductor over not more than 4 ft of roof measured horizontally) to a through-the-roof raceway or approved support, the clearance may be 18 in.

Overhead service conductors must clear finished grade by at least 10 ft at the service entrance, at the lowest point of the drip loop, and over areas accessible only to pedestrians (150 V or less to ground, cabled with a messenger).

Overhead conductors need 12 ft clearance over residential property and driveways and commercial areas not subject to truck traffic (300 V or less to ground), or 15 ft for those areas when over 300 V to ground.
Overhead conductors need 18 ft clearance over public streets, alleys, roads, parking areas subject to truck traffic and non-residential driveways, and 24-1/2 ft over railroad tracks.
Overhead feeder and branch-circuit conductors (outside wiring) must have at least 8 ft 6 in clearance above roofs, with exceptions similar to those for services.

Service conductors must have at least 3 ft clearance from windows that open, doors, porches, balconies, ladders, stairs and fire escapes; conductors run above the top of a window are considered out of reach.
The point of attachment of overhead service conductors to a building must be at least 10 ft above finished grade.
Overhead and underground service conductors must be at least 8 AWG copper or 6 AWG aluminum or copper-clad aluminum (12 AWG is allowed only for limited loads).
Minimum service disconnect ratings: one-family dwelling 100 A, 3-wire; single-circuit installation 15 A; two-circuit installation 30 A; all other installations 60 A.
The service disconnecting means must be at a readily accessible location either outside the building or inside nearest the point of entrance of the service conductors.

A service may have one disconnect, or two to six disconnects only if each is in a separate enclosure, a panelboard with its own main, a switchboard section with barriers, or a separate switchgear/metering compartment. Since NEC 2020, up to six disconnects in one common enclosure (such as handle-tied single-pole breakers in one panel) are no longer allowed.
Where two to six service disconnects are used they must be grouped, and each must be marked to indicate the load it serves.

One- and two-family dwellings need an emergency disconnect at a readily accessible outdoor location on or within sight of the dwelling: the service disconnect, a meter disconnect, or another listed disconnect suitable for service equipment on the supply side. It is marked 'EMERGENCY DISCONNECT' (plus 'SERVICE DISCONNECT' or 'NOT SERVICE EQUIPMENT' as applicable). First required in NEC 2020.

NEC 2023 requires the emergency disconnect marking to be on the outside front of the enclosure, with a red background, white text and letters at least 1/2 in high, and replaced service equipment must also comply.

Services supplying dwelling units must have a Type 1 or Type 2 surge-protective device (SPD) integral to or adjacent to the service equipment (first required in NEC 2020). NEC 2023 extends this to dormitory units, hotel guest rooms and suites, and nursing home/limited-care patient sleeping rooms, requires a nominal discharge current rating of at least 10 kA, and applies when service equipment is replaced.

New in NEC 2023, feeders supplying dwelling units, dormitory units, guest rooms and suites, and nursing home patient sleeping rooms also need a Type 1 or Type 2 SPD rated at least 10 kA in or adjacent to the distribution equipment.

Service equipment must have barriers so no one can accidentally contact uninsulated, ungrounded busbars or terminals that stay energized on the line side when the service disconnect is open (added in NEC 2020).
Service conductors may not share a raceway or cable with feeder or branch-circuit conductors; grounding electrode conductors and supply-side bonding jumpers are permitted with them.

A building is generally supplied by only one service. Exceptions include fire pumps, emergency/standby systems, parallel power production, multiple-occupancy buildings, and capacity needs such as loads over 2000 A at 1000 V or less.
Service heads must be located above the point of attachment of the service-drop conductors (or within 24 in of it where impracticable), and drip loops must be formed on the conductors.

A building supplied from another building is generally fed by one feeder or branch circuit, with its disconnect at a readily accessible location nearest the point of entrance (or outside), and no more than six disconnects grouped together.
New in NEC 2023, one- and two-family dwellings supplied by a feeder (not a service) need an outdoor emergency disconnect similar to the 230.85 requirement for services.

Where a conductor's ampacity does not match a standard OCPD rating, the next higher standard rating is allowed, up to 800 A, as long as the conductors do not supply a multioutlet branch circuit for cord-and-plug loads. Example: 500 kcmil Cu at 75 C (380 A) may be protected at 400 A.
If the overcurrent device is rated over 800 A, the conductor ampacity must be equal to or greater than the OCPD rating (no rounding up).

Small-conductor overcurrent limits: 14 AWG copper 15 A, 10 AWG copper 30 A, 12 AWG aluminum/copper-clad aluminum 15 A, 10 AWG aluminum/copper-clad aluminum 25 A (unless specifically permitted elsewhere, such as motor circuits).

18 AWG copper may be protected at 7 A and 16 AWG copper at 10 A only under specific conditions, such as continuous loads not over 5.6 A (18 AWG) or 8 A (16 AWG) and specific listed overcurrent devices.

10 ft feeder tap rule: tap conductors no longer than 10 ft must have ampacity not less than the calculated load and not less than the rating of the device they supply; for field installations leaving the enclosure, ampacity must be at least 10% of the feeder OCPD rating.

25 ft feeder tap rule: tap ampacity must be at least 1/3 of the feeder OCPD rating, and the tap must end in a single breaker or set of fuses that limits the load to the tap ampacity. Example: a 300 A feeder needs 25 ft tap conductors of at least 100 A.

Transformer secondary conductors up to 25 ft long: their ampacity, multiplied by the secondary-to-primary voltage ratio, must be at least 1/3 of the primary OCPD rating, and they must terminate in a single OCPD limiting load to their ampacity.
Overcurrent devices must be readily accessible, with the center of the operating handle grip, in its highest position, no more than 6 ft 7 in above the floor or working platform.

Overcurrent devices may not be located near easily ignitible material such as in clothes closets, or over steps of a stairway. They may not be in bathrooms of dwellings, dormitories or guest rooms; NEC 2023 extends this to all bathrooms, showering facilities and locker rooms with showers.
Individual single-pole breakers with identified handle ties may protect multiwire branch circuits serving only line-to-neutral loads, and line-to-line single-phase loads where permitted.
Circuit breakers used as switches for 120 V and 277 V fluorescent lighting circuits must be listed and marked SWD or HID (HID-marked breakers for high-intensity discharge lighting).

Where the highest continuous current trip setting of a circuit breaker is 1200 A or higher, a method to reduce clearing time (arc energy reduction) is required, such as zone-selective interlocking, differential relaying, an energy-reducing maintenance switch, or active arc-flash mitigation.

Plug fuses may be used only in circuits not exceeding 125 V between conductors (or 150 V to ground on grounded-neutral systems). Edison-base plug fuses may be used only as replacements in existing installations; new work uses Type S fuses.
A metal underground water pipe qualifies as a grounding electrode if it is in direct contact with the earth for 10 ft or more, but it must always be supplemented by an additional electrode.

A concrete-encased electrode (Ufer) is at least 20 ft of bare or conductively coated steel reinforcing bar at least 1/2 in diameter, or at least 20 ft of bare copper not smaller than 4 AWG, encased in at least 2 in of concrete that is in direct contact with the earth.

If a concrete-encased electrode is present at a building or structure, it must be bonded into the grounding electrode system (existing buildings are exempt where the rebar can't be reached without disturbing the concrete).
A ground ring electrode encircles the building, is in direct contact with the earth, consists of at least 20 ft of bare copper not smaller than 2 AWG, and is buried at least 30 in deep.

Rod and pipe electrodes must be at least 8 ft long. Pipe or conduit electrodes must be at least 3/4 trade size (galvanized or otherwise corrosion protected); rods must be at least 5/8 in diameter unless listed (listed rods may be 1/2 in).

A ground rod must have at least 8 ft in contact with soil and be driven vertically; if rock is hit it may be driven at an angle no more than 45 degrees from vertical or buried in a trench at least 30 in deep. The top must be flush with or below grade unless protected.
A single rod, pipe or plate electrode must be supplemented by an additional electrode unless the single electrode has a resistance to earth of 25 ohms or less.
When multiple rod, pipe or plate electrodes are used, they must be at least 6 ft apart (and at least 6 ft from electrodes of other grounding systems, such as lightning protection).

A plate electrode must expose at least 2 sq ft of surface to the soil; iron or steel plates must be at least 1/4 in thick, nonferrous plates at least 0.06 in thick, and plates are buried at least 30 in below the surface.
Metal underground gas piping, aluminum, and swimming pool structures and reinforcing steel (680.26(B)(1) and (B)(2)) may not be used as grounding electrodes.
Interior metal water piping located not more than 5 ft from the point of entrance to the building may be used as a conductor to interconnect electrodes of the grounding electrode system.

GEC sizing: for largest service conductors of 2 AWG or smaller copper (1/0 or smaller aluminum), the GEC is 8 AWG copper or 6 AWG aluminum; for 1 or 1/0 copper (2/0 or 3/0 aluminum), 6 AWG copper or 4 AWG aluminum.

GEC sizing: for 2/0 or 3/0 copper service conductors (4/0 or 250 kcmil aluminum) the GEC is 4 AWG copper or 2 AWG aluminum; for over 3/0 through 350 kcmil copper (over 250 through 500 kcmil aluminum) it is 2 AWG copper or 1/0 aluminum.

GEC sizing: over 350 through 600 kcmil copper calls for 1/0 copper (3/0 aluminum); over 600 through 1100 kcmil copper calls for 2/0 copper (4/0 aluminum); over 1100 kcmil copper calls for 3/0 copper (250 kcmil aluminum).
The portion of a GEC that is the sole connection to a rod, pipe or plate electrode does not need to be larger than 6 AWG copper or 4 AWG aluminum, regardless of service size.
A GEC that is the sole connection to a concrete-encased electrode need not be larger than 4 AWG copper; one that is the sole connection to a ground ring need not be larger than the ring conductor.
Example: a 200 A service with 2/0 copper (or 4/0 aluminum) conductors needs a 4 AWG copper GEC to the water pipe, but the jumper to a ground rod need not exceed 6 AWG copper.

A 6 AWG or larger copper GEC may run along a building surface without protection if securely fastened and not exposed to physical damage; an 8 AWG GEC must be protected in RMC, IMC, PVC, RTRC, EMT or cable armor.
A GEC must be installed in one continuous length without a splice, except splices made with irreversible compression connectors or exothermic welding, or connections to a busbar.
A ferrous (steel) raceway enclosing a GEC must be bonded at each end to the GEC so the raceway and conductor are electrically parallel.
GEC connections to electrodes must be accessible, except connections to concrete-encased, driven or buried electrodes, which need not be accessible.

The grounded (neutral) service conductor must be brought to each service disconnect and be at least the size in Table 250.102(C)(1) (same sizes as Table 250.66 up to 1100 kcmil copper); above that, it must be at least 12.5% of the area of the largest ungrounded conductor.

The main bonding jumper is sized from Table 250.102(C)(1); for service conductors larger than 1100 kcmil copper, it must be at least 12.5% of the largest phase conductor area. Example: 4 x 500 kcmil per phase (2000 kcmil) requires a 250 kcmil copper main bonding jumper.

The grounded (neutral) conductor may not be connected to equipment grounding conductors or grounding electrodes on the load side of the service disconnect (with limited exceptions), so neutrals and grounds are kept separate in subpanels.

A building supplied by a feeder or branch circuit must have its own grounding electrode system, except where it is supplied by a single branch circuit (including a multiwire branch circuit) that includes an equipment grounding conductor.

At a separate building supplied by a feeder, an equipment grounding conductor is run with the feeder and the grounded (neutral) conductor is not connected to the grounding system there (no neutral-to-ground bond), except for certain existing installations.

A separately derived system (such as a transformer) needs a system bonding jumper connecting the grounded conductor to the supply-side bonding jumper or enclosure at one point (the source or the first disconnect), and a GEC sized from Table 250.66 based on the derived ungrounded conductors.

AC systems of 50 to 1000 V must be grounded where the maximum voltage to ground is 150 V or less, where the system is 3-phase 4-wire wye with the neutral used as a circuit conductor, or where it is 3-phase 4-wire delta with the midpoint of one phase used as a circuit conductor.
Electrical equipment and wiring must provide an effective low-impedance ground-fault current path; the earth may not be considered an effective ground-fault current path.
Minimum EGC size by OCPD rating: 15 A, 14 AWG copper (12 AWG aluminum); 30 A through 60 A, 10 AWG copper (8 AWG aluminum); 100 A, 8 AWG copper (6 AWG aluminum).

Minimum EGC size by OCPD rating: 200 A, 6 AWG copper (4 AWG aluminum); 300 A, 4 AWG copper; 400 A, 3 AWG copper (1 AWG aluminum); 600 A, 1 AWG copper; 800 A, 1/0 copper; 1000 A, 2/0 copper; 1200 A, 3/0 copper.

If ungrounded conductors are increased in size (for example for voltage drop), the EGC must be increased proportionally by circular-mil area. Example: upsizing a 20 A circuit from 12 AWG (6,530 cmil) to 10 AWG (10,380 cmil) is a 1.59 ratio, so the 12 AWG EGC becomes 10 AWG.
When parallel conductors run in multiple raceways or cables, a full-size EGC (based on the OCPD rating per Table 250.122) is required in each raceway or cable.

Permitted EGC types include the wire itself, RMC, IMC, EMT, the armor of Type AC cable, and qualifying MC cable armor. Flexible metal conduit counts only with listed fittings on circuits of 20 A or less with a total ground-return length of 6 ft or less.

Liquidtight flexible metal conduit may serve as an EGC only in lengths totaling 6 ft or less with listed fittings: trade sizes 3/8 through 1/2 on circuits of 20 A or less, and 3/4 through 1-1/4 on circuits of 60 A or less, and not where installed for flexibility after installation.

Interior metal water piping must be bonded to the service equipment enclosure, the grounded conductor at the service, the GEC (if large enough) or the electrodes, using a bonding jumper sized from Table 250.102(C)(1).

Other metal piping that may become energized, such as gas piping, must be bonded; the equipment grounding conductor of the circuit likely to energize it (for example a gas furnace circuit) may serve as the bonding means.

An intersystem bonding termination with capacity for at least three intersystem bonding conductors (for communications systems such as telephone, CATV and satellite) is required at the service equipment or metering equipment, accessible and outside enclosures.

Service raceways and enclosures must be bonded with threaded couplings or hubs made wrenchtight, threadless couplings made tight, listed bonding devices (bonding locknuts, wedges, bushings) or bonding jumpers; standard locknuts alone are not acceptable where concentric or eccentric knockouts are impaired.

For circuits over 250 V to ground (such as 277/480 V), metal raceways and cables must be bonded around concentric or eccentric knockouts with bonding jumpers or listed fittings, unless the knockouts are not impaired.

A bonding jumper from the box to the receptacle grounding terminal is required, except for surface boxes with direct metal-to-metal contact, receptacles listed as self-grounding, certain listed floor boxes, and isolated-ground receptacles.

Grounding and bonding connections must use listed pressure connectors, terminal bars, exothermic welding, machine screws or thread-forming screws engaging at least two threads, or other listed means; sheet metal screws may not be used.

Nonconductive coatings such as paint, lacquer and enamel must be removed at threads, contact points and contact surfaces where grounding or bonding connections are made (or fittings must make removal unnecessary).
Aluminum or copper-clad aluminum GECs may not be used in direct contact with masonry or earth or where subject to corrosion, and outdoors they must terminate at least 18 in above the earth.
All EGCs in a box must be connected together, and the connection must be arranged so that removing a receptacle or device does not interrupt EGC continuity.

In residential occupancies, cord-and-plug-connected refrigerators, freezers, air conditioners, clothes washers and dryers, dishwashers, ranges, disposers, sump pumps, aquarium equipment and hand-held, stationary or landscape tools must have their exposed metal grounded, except listed double-insulated tools and appliances.

All conductors of the same circuit, including the grounded conductor and all equipment grounding and bonding conductors, must be in the same raceway, cable, trench, cord or cable tray (with exceptions such as parallel runs).

Holes bored through wood framing for cables or raceways must have their edge at least 1-1/4 in from the nearest edge of the wood; otherwise a steel plate or sleeve at least 1/16 in thick must protect the cable. The same applies to notches.
Where NM cable passes through factory or field openings in metal framing, listed bushings or grommets covering all metal edges must be securely fastened in the openings before the cable is installed.
Cables or raceways run parallel to framing members must be at least 1-1/4 in from the nearest edge of the member, or be protected by a steel plate at least 1/16 in thick.
Cables and raceways under metal-corrugated sheet roof decking must be at least 1-1/2 in from the lowest surface of the decking, and may not be installed in concealed locations of the decking itself.

Where raceways contain 4 AWG or larger insulated circuit conductors entering a cabinet, box or enclosure, the conductors must be protected by an identified fitting with a smoothly rounded insulating surface, such as an insulated bushing.

Direct-buried conductors and cables emerging from grade must be protected by enclosures or raceways from the required cover depth (not more than 18 in required) up to at least 8 ft above finished grade.
Underground service conductors that are not encased in concrete and are buried 18 in or more below grade need a warning ribbon placed in the trench at least 12 in above the installation.
Cover is the distance from the top of a buried conductor, cable or raceway to the top of finished grade, concrete or similar cover.
Minimum cover in general locations: direct-burial cables 24 in; RMC or IMC 6 in; nonmetallic raceway listed for direct burial without concrete encasement 18 in.

Minimum cover for residential branch circuits of 120 V or less with GFCI protection and 20 A maximum overcurrent protection is 12 in; for irrigation and landscape lighting circuits limited to 30 V installed with UF or identified cable, 6 in.
Under streets, highways, roads, alleys, driveways and parking lots, the minimum cover is 24 in for every wiring method in the table.

Under one- and two-family dwelling driveways and outdoor parking areas used only for dwelling purposes, minimum cover is 18 in for direct burial, RMC/IMC, nonmetallic raceway and landscape circuits, and 12 in for 20 A GFCI-protected residential branch circuits.

In a trench below at least 2 in of concrete or equivalent, minimum cover is 18 in for direct-burial cable, 6 in for RMC/IMC, 12 in for nonmetallic raceway, and 6 in for GFCI-protected residential circuits and landscape circuits.

At least 6 in of free conductor must be left at each box for splices or device connections, and where the box opening is less than 8 in in any dimension, at least 3 in must extend outside the opening.
The interior of a raceway in a wet location above grade is considered a wet location, so conductors inside must be listed for wet locations (for example THWN).

Raceways passing between areas of very different temperature must be sealed to prevent warm air circulating to the colder part, and expansion fittings must be used where needed for thermal expansion and contraction.

Ceiling support wires that hold up a suspended ceiling may not support wiring unless they are independent support wires, secured at both ends and identified; ceiling grids may not support wiring unless listed for it.
Raceways may not be used as a means of support for other raceways, cables or nonelectrical equipment (an exception allows Class 2 control cable supported by the raceway supplying that equipment).
In ferrous metal raceways or enclosures, all phase conductors, the grounded conductor (if used) and EGCs of a circuit must be grouped together to avoid heating by induction.
Electrical penetrations through fire-resistance-rated walls, partitions, floors and ceilings must be firestopped with approved methods that maintain the fire rating.

In laundries, canneries, dairies and other indoor wet locations or where walls are frequently washed, the wiring system (boxes, fittings, raceways, cables) must be mounted with at least a 1/4 in air space from the wall or supporting surface.
A box or conduit body is required at each splice point, outlet point, switch point, junction point, termination point or pull point (with listed exceptions).
Table 310.16 ampacities assume not more than three current-carrying conductors in a raceway, cable or earth, at an ambient temperature of 30 C (86 F).
Copper ampacities (60 C / 75 C / 90 C): 14 AWG 15/20/25 A; 10 AWG 30/35/40 A; 8 AWG 40/50/55 A.
Aluminum ampacities at 75 C: 8 AWG 40 A; 6 AWG 50 A; 4 AWG 65 A; 2 AWG 90 A; 1/0 120 A; 2/0 135 A; 3/0 155 A; 4/0 180 A; 250 kcmil 205 A; 350 kcmil 250 A; 500 kcmil 310 A.
Ambient temperature correction (30 C base) for 36-40 C (97-104 F): 0.82 for 60 C conductors, 0.88 for 75 C, and 0.91 for 90 C.
Adjustment factors for more than three current-carrying conductors: 4-6 conductors 80%; 7-9 conductors 70%; 10-20 conductors 50%; 21-30 conductors 45%; 31-40 conductors 40%; 41 or more 35%.
Adjustment factors for more than three current-carrying conductors do not apply to conductors in raceways (nipples) 24 in or less in length.
Example: nine 12 AWG THHN current-carrying conductors in one conduit at 30 C: 30 A (90 C column) x 0.70 = 21 A ampacity, but 240.4(D) still limits the overcurrent device to 20 A.
Example: six 10 AWG THHN current-carrying conductors at 40 C ambient: 40 A (90 C) x 0.80 x 0.91 = 29.1 A adjusted ampacity.

A neutral that carries only the unbalanced current of its circuit is not counted as current-carrying, but it is counted on a 3-wire circuit (two phases and neutral) of a 4-wire 3-phase wye system, and on a 4-wire 3-phase wye circuit where most of the load is nonlinear.
Equipment grounding and bonding conductors are not counted as current-carrying conductors when applying adjustment factors.

Raceways or cables exposed to sunlight on or above rooftops less than 7/8 in above the roof must have 33 C (60 F) added to the outdoor ambient temperature for correction; Type XHHW-2 conductors are exempt.

For a 120/240 V single-phase service or feeder rated 100-400 A supplying the entire load of a one-family dwelling (or individual dwelling unit), conductors may have an ampacity of not less than 83% of the rating. Example: 200 A x 0.83 = 166 A, so 2/0 copper or 4/0 aluminum (75 C) is permitted.

The 83% dwelling service rule does not override ambient temperature correction or adjustment factors; where they apply, take 83% of the rating and then apply the correction/adjustment before choosing the conductor.
Conductors may be run in parallel only in sizes 1/0 AWG and larger, and each parallel set must be the same length, conductor material, size, insulation type and terminated in the same manner.
Where different ampacities apply to portions of a circuit, the higher ampacity may be used if the lower-ampacity portion does not exceed the lesser of 10 ft or 10% of the total circuit length.
Insulation ratings: THHN 90 C dry and damp; THWN 75 C wet or dry; THWN-2 and XHHW-2 90 C wet or dry; XHHW 90 C dry, 75 C wet; THW 75 C; UF cable 60 C.
The minimum general-use conductor size for 600 V and below is 14 AWG copper and 12 AWG aluminum or copper-clad aluminum (smaller sizes only where specifically permitted elsewhere).
facts.note: NEC 2023 also recognizes 14 AWG copper-clad aluminum for the new 10 A circuits; confirm details in 310.3/240.4(D).

facts.fact: For box fill, each conductor that originates outside the box and terminates or is spliced inside counts as one; a conductor passing through unbroken counts as one; an unbroken loop or coil at least twice the 6 in minimum free length (12 in) counts as two. Conductors that never leave the box, such as pigtails, are not counted.
For box fill, one or more internal cable clamps together count as one volume allowance based on the largest conductor, and each type of support fitting (fixture stud or hickey) counts as one.

For box fill, each yoke or strap holding one or more devices (switch or receptacle) counts as two volume allowances based on the largest conductor connected to the device; a device wider than a single 2 in device box counts as two for each gang required.
For box fill, all equipment grounding conductors together count as one volume allowance based on the largest EGC; an additional set of isolated EGCs counts as one more.
Up to four fixture wires smaller than 14 AWG (plus an EGC) entering the box from a domed luminaire canopy may be left out of the box fill count.
Box fill volume per conductor: 18 AWG 1.50 cu in; 16 AWG 1.75 cu in; 8 AWG 3.00 cu in; 6 AWG 5.00 cu in.
Standard metal box volumes: 4 x 1-1/2 in square 21.0 cu in; 4 x 2-1/8 in square 30.3 cu in; 4-11/16 x 1-1/2 in square 29.5 cu in; 4-11/16 x 2-1/8 in square 42.0 cu in.
More box volumes: 4 x 1-1/2 in octagon 15.5 cu in; 4 x 2-1/8 in octagon 21.5 cu in; 3 x 2 x 2-1/2 in device box 12.5 cu in; 3 x 2 x 3-1/2 in device box 18.0 cu in.

Example: a single-gang box with two 12/2 NM cables, one receptacle and internal clamps counts 4 insulated conductors + 1 (grounds) + 1 (clamps) + 2 (device) = 8 allowances x 2.25 cu in = 18.0 cu in required.
A 4 x 2-1/8 in square box (30.3 cu in) may hold at most 15 conductors of 14 AWG or 13 conductors of 12 AWG (30.3 / 2.25 = 13.4, rounded down).
Straight-pull boxes for conductors 4 AWG and larger must be at least 8 times the trade size of the largest raceway long. Example: a 3 in conduit needs a box at least 24 in long.

For angle or U pulls (4 AWG and larger), the distance from the raceway entry to the opposite wall must be at least 6 times the trade size of the largest raceway in the row plus the sum of the other raceways in that row; raceway entries enclosing the same conductor must be at least 6 times the larger raceway apart. Example: 3 in + 2 in on one wall: 6 x 3 + 2 = 20 in.

In noncombustible walls or ceilings (concrete, tile, gypsum, plaster), boxes may be set back no more than 1/4 in from the finished surface; in combustible surfaces such as wood, boxes must be flush with or project from the surface.
Plaster, drywall or plasterboard that is broken or incomplete around a box must be repaired so there are no gaps or open spaces larger than 1/8 in at the edge of the box.

Ceiling outlet boxes for luminaires must be designed to support a luminaire of at least 50 lb; luminaires heavier than 50 lb must be supported independently unless the box is listed and marked for the weight.

Boxes used as the sole support of ceiling-suspended (paddle) fans must be listed for fan support up to 70 lb, and boxes for fans over 35 lb must be marked with the maximum weight. Ceiling boxes in dwelling habitable rooms where a fan could be installed must be listed for fan support.

A box supported only by raceways needs two or more conduits threaded wrenchtight, secured within 3 ft of the box (enclosures without devices or luminaires) or within 18 in (enclosures with devices or luminaires).

NM cable entering a single-gang nonmetallic box (not larger than 2-1/4 x 4 in) need not be clamped to the box if the cable is fastened within 8 in of the box and the sheath extends at least 1/4 in inside the box.

Conductors (including splices and taps) in switch and overcurrent device enclosures may not fill more than 40% of the cross-sectional area, and splices and taps may not fill more than 75% of the area at any cross section.
Outlet and device boxes must be at least 1/2 in deep inside; where utilization equipment projects more than 1-7/8 in into the box, the box depth must be the projection plus 1/4 in.

Conductors in a metal wireway may not exceed 20% of the interior cross-sectional area (splices and taps 75%); adjustment factors apply only when there are more than 30 current-carrying conductors at any cross section; wireways are supported at intervals not exceeding 5 ft.
NM cable must be secured at intervals not exceeding 4-1/2 ft and within 12 in of every cabinet, box or fitting.
NM cable run horizontally through bored holes or notches in framing spaced not more than 4-1/2 ft apart is considered supported and secured.
NM cable and AC cable may not be bent to a radius less than 5 times the cable diameter.
NM cable ampacity is limited to the 60 C conductor rating; the 90 C rating may be used for adjustment and correction calculations, but the final ampacity may not exceed the 60 C value.

NM cable is permitted in one- and two-family dwellings and their garages and storage buildings, in multifamily dwellings of Type III, IV or V construction, and in other Type III, IV or V structures when concealed behind a thermal barrier with at least a 15-minute finish rating.
NM cable may not be used as service-entrance cable, embedded in concrete or masonry, in hazardous locations, exposed to corrosive fumes, or in wet or damp locations.

In unfinished basements and crawl spaces, NM cable smaller than two 6 AWG or three 8 AWG conductors must run through bored holes in joists or on running boards; larger cables may be secured directly to the lower edges of joists.

In attics reached by permanent stairs or ladders, cables run across the tops of joists, or within 7 ft of the floor or joists across the face of rafters or studs, need guard strips at least as high as the cable; without permanent stairs or ladders, protection is required only within 6 ft of the scuttle hole or attic entrance.

AC (armored) cable must be secured within 12 in of every box and at intervals not exceeding 4-1/2 ft; it may be unsupported up to 2 ft at terminals where flexibility is needed, and up to 6 ft from the last support to a luminaire in an accessible ceiling.
An insulating bushing (anti-short bushing, or 'redhead') is required at the ends of AC cable between the conductors and the armor.

MC cable must be supported and secured at intervals not exceeding 6 ft; MC with four or fewer conductors no larger than 10 AWG must be secured within 12 in of every box or fitting; it may be unsupported up to 6 ft to a luminaire or equipment in an accessible ceiling.
EMT must be securely fastened within 3 ft of each outlet box, junction box, cabinet, conduit body or other termination and supported at intervals not exceeding 10 ft.
Between pull points (boxes, conduit bodies), EMT, RMC, IMC and PVC runs may not have more than the equivalent of four quarter bends, 360 degrees total.
EMT smaller than 1/2 trade size may not be used (except enclosing motor leads), and the largest EMT permitted is 4 trade size.

RMC must be secured within 3 ft of each box or termination and supported at least every 10 ft; straight runs with threaded couplings may be supported per Table 344.30(B)(2): 1/2-3/4 in 10 ft, 1 in 12 ft, 1-1/4 to 1-1/2 in 14 ft, 2-2-1/2 in 16 ft, 3 in and larger 20 ft.
PVC conduit must be secured within 3 ft of each box and supported at maximum spacings of 3 ft (1/2-1 in), 5 ft (1-1/4 to 2 in), 6 ft (2-1/2 to 3 in), 7 ft (3-1/2 to 5 in) and 8 ft (6 in).
PVC conduit needs expansion fittings where the expected length change from thermal expansion or contraction is 1/4 in or more in a straight run between securely mounted items such as boxes.
PVC conduit exposed to physical damage must be identified for that use, such as Schedule 80.

Flexible metal conduit and liquidtight flexible metal conduit must be secured within 12 in of each box and at intervals not exceeding 4-1/2 ft; unsupported lengths are allowed up to 3 ft (1/2-1-1/4 trade size), 4 ft (1-1/2-2) or 5 ft (2-1/2 and larger) at terminals where flexibility is needed, and up to 6 ft for luminaire whips in accessible ceilings.
ENT (electrical nonmetallic tubing) must be secured within 3 ft of each box and at intervals not exceeding 3 ft.
In buildings exceeding three floors above grade, ENT must be concealed in walls, floors and ceilings behind a thermal barrier with at least a 15-minute finish rating.
LFNC-B (liquidtight flexible nonmetallic conduit) must be secured within 12 in of each box and at intervals not exceeding 3 ft.

Type UF cable may be directly buried, but may not be used as service-entrance cable, embedded in poured concrete, or exposed to direct sunlight unless identified as sunlight resistant; its ampacity is based on 60 C conductors.
Maximum conduit fill: 53% of the cross-sectional area for one conductor, 31% for two conductors, and 40% for more than two conductors.
A conduit or tubing nipple 24 in or less long between boxes may be filled to 60% of its total cross-sectional area, and ampacity adjustment factors do not apply to it.
Equipment grounding and bonding conductors must be included when calculating conduit fill, using their actual dimensions.
When calculating the number of same-size conductors in a raceway, a result with a decimal of 0.8 or larger may be rounded up to the next whole number.
EMT 40% fill areas: 1/2 trade size 0.122 sq in; 3/4 0.213 sq in; 1 in 0.346 sq in; 1-1/4 0.598 sq in; 1-1/2 0.814 sq in; 2 in 1.342 sq in.
Approximate areas of THHN/THWN-2 conductors: 14 AWG 0.0097 sq in; 12 AWG 0.0133; 10 AWG 0.0211; 8 AWG 0.0366; 6 AWG 0.0507.
Approximate areas of THHN/THWN-2 conductors: 4 AWG 0.0824 sq in; 3 AWG 0.0973; 2 AWG 0.1158; 1 AWG 0.1562; 1/0 0.1855; 2/0 0.2223; 3/0 0.2679; 4/0 0.3237.

facts.source: NEC 2023 Chapter 9 Tables 4 and 5; Annex C Table C.1
facts.fact: Maximum THHN conductors in EMT: 1/2 in EMT holds 12 of 14 AWG, 9 of 12 AWG or 5 of 10 AWG; 3/4 in EMT holds 22 of 14 AWG, 16 of 12 AWG or 10 of 10 AWG.
Example: three 6 AWG THHN (3 x 0.0507) plus one 10 AWG THHN (0.0211) total 0.1732 sq in, which fits 3/4 in EMT (0.213 sq in at 40%) but not 1/2 in EMT (0.122 sq in).
DC resistance of uncoated copper at 75 C per 1,000 ft: 14 AWG 3.07 ohms solid / 3.14 stranded; 12 AWG 1.93 solid / 1.98 stranded; 10 AWG 1.21 solid / 1.24 stranded; 8 AWG 0.778 stranded.
Conductors 250 and larger are sized in kcmil, where 1 kcmil = 1,000 circular mils (250 kcmil = 250,000 cmil); the AWG scale ends at 4/0 (211,600 cmil).

Switches and circuit breakers used as switches must be readily accessible, with the center of the operating handle grip, in its highest position, no more than 6 ft 7 in above the floor or working platform.

A grounded (neutral) conductor must be provided at most switch locations that control lighting loads (for example in habitable rooms, bathrooms, hallways and stairways), with limited exceptions, so electronic controls can be installed.
An AC general-use snap switch may control resistive and inductive loads up to its ampere rating, but motor loads may not exceed 80% of its ampere rating at rated voltage.
Switches may not be installed within tub or shower spaces unless installed as part of a listed tub or shower assembly.
Snap switches, including dimmers, must be connected to an equipment grounding conductor, and metal faceplates must be grounded.
Single-throw knife switches, molded-case switches and circuit breakers used as switches must be connected so their blades are de-energized when the switch is open (line on the stationary side).
General-use and motor-circuit switches and circuit breakers must clearly indicate whether they are on or off; when operated vertically, up must be the on position.

Every circuit and circuit modification must be legibly identified at its panelboard as to its clear, evident and specific purpose; descriptions may not depend on transient conditions of occupancy (such as a person's name).
Each panelboard must be protected by an overcurrent device with a rating not greater than that of the panelboard, located within or on the supply side of the panelboard.
On a 3-phase, 4-wire delta system, the phase with the higher voltage to ground (high leg) must be the B phase (center position) in panelboards and switchboards.
Each grounded (neutral) conductor in a panelboard must terminate in an individual terminal that is not also used for another conductor.
Panelboards may not be installed in a face-up position.

Closet luminaire clearances from the storage space: surface-mounted incandescent or LED with a completely enclosed light source, 12 in; surface-mounted fluorescent, 6 in; recessed incandescent or LED with a completely enclosed source, 6 in; recessed fluorescent, 6 in. Surface fluorescent or LED luminaires identified for use within the storage area may be installed there.
Incandescent luminaires with open or partially enclosed lamps, and pendant luminaires or lampholders, are not permitted in clothes closets.

No cord-connected luminaires, chain-, cable- or cord-suspended luminaires, lighting track, pendants or ceiling paddle fans may be within 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of a bathtub rim or shower threshold. Luminaires in that zone must be listed for damp locations, or wet locations where subject to shower spray.
facts.note: NEC 2023 moved the paddle-fan portion to 422.18(B); the 3 ft / 8 ft zone is unchanged.

facts.fact: A recessed luminaire that is not Type IC must have at least 1/2 in clearance from combustible materials (except at support points), and thermal insulation may not be within 3 in of its enclosure, wiring compartment, ballast or driver.

Luminaires in suspended ceilings must be secured to the ceiling framing members by bolts, screws, rivets or listed clips identified for the purpose, and the framing must be fastened to each other and to the building structure.

In indoor locations other than dwellings, fluorescent luminaires with double-ended lamps and ballasts serviced in place need a disconnecting means so ballasts can be replaced without working on energized parts.

Cord lengths: in-sink waste disposers 18 to 36 in; built-in dishwashers and trash compactors 3 to 4 ft (measured from the plug face to the rear of the appliance); range hoods 18 to 36 in. Receptacles must be accessible and located to avoid damage to the cord.

For a single non-motor-operated appliance, the OCPD may not exceed the rating marked on the appliance; if unmarked, it may not exceed 20 A for appliances rated 13.3 A or less, or 150% of rated current for appliances over 13.3 A (next higher standard size permitted).
Resistance heating appliances and fixed space heaters rated over 48 A must have their elements subdivided into loads of not more than 48 A, each protected at not more than 60 A.

A fixed storage-type water heater of 120 gallons or less is considered a continuous load, so its branch circuit must be rated at least 125% of the nameplate. Example: 4500 W / 240 V = 18.75 A x 1.25 = 23.4 A, so at least a 25 A circuit, which needs 10 AWG copper because 240.4(D) limits 12 AWG to 20 A.

For permanently connected appliances rated 300 VA or 1/8 hp or less, the branch-circuit OCPD may serve as the disconnect; for larger appliances, the branch-circuit switch or breaker may serve if it is within sight or lockable in the open position.

Central heating equipment (other than fixed electric space heating) must be on an individual branch circuit; directly associated auxiliary equipment such as pumps, valves, humidifiers and electrostatic air cleaners may share it.

Fixed electric space-heating equipment is considered a continuous load, so branch-circuit conductors and OCPDs are sized at 125% of the load. Example: 10 kW at 240 V = 41.7 A x 1.25 = 52.1 A, so a 60 A breaker with 6 AWG copper.

Permanently installed electric baseboard heaters with factory-installed receptacles (or listed receptacle assemblies) may count toward required receptacle outlets, but those receptacles may not be connected to the heater circuit; listing instructions may prohibit receptacles above baseboard heaters.

Fixed electric space heating must have a means to simultaneously disconnect the heater, motor controller(s) and supplementary overcurrent devices from all ungrounded conductors, located within sight or lockable in the open position.

Motor conductor ampacity, switch ratings and short-circuit/ground-fault protection are based on the full-load current values in Tables 430.247-430.250, not the nameplate; separate overload protection is based on the motor nameplate full-load current.
Branch-circuit conductors for a single continuous-duty motor must have an ampacity of at least 125% of the motor's full-load current from the tables.
Conductors supplying several motors must be sized for at least 125% of the largest motor's FLC, plus the FLC of all other motors, plus 100% of noncontinuous and 125% of continuous non-motor loads.
Example: three 460 V, 3-phase motors of 10 hp (14 A), 15 hp (21 A) and 20 hp (27 A) need feeder conductors of at least 27 x 1.25 + 14 + 21 = 68.75 A.

Separate overload devices for continuous-duty motors over 1 hp are sized at no more than 125% of nameplate FLA for motors with a service factor of 1.15 or more or a temperature rise of 40 C or less, and 115% for all other motors.

If the overload chosen under 430.32(A)(1) will not let the motor start or carry its load, the next higher size may be used, up to 140% of nameplate FLA (service factor 1.15+ or temp rise 40 C or less) or 130% for all other motors.

Maximum motor branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection, as a percent of FLC, for single-phase and polyphase AC motors (other than wound-rotor): nontime-delay fuse 300%; dual-element (time-delay) fuse 175%; instantaneous-trip breaker 800%; inverse-time breaker 250%.
If the percentage from Table 430.52 does not give a standard fuse or breaker size, the next higher standard size may be used.

If the Table 430.52 rating will not allow the motor to start, it may be increased: nontime-delay fuses (600 A or less) up to 400%; time-delay fuses up to 225%; inverse-time breakers up to 400% for FLC of 100 A or less and 300% for FLC over 100 A.

Example: a 10 hp, 230 V, 3-phase motor (28 A) needs conductors of at least 35 A (28 x 1.25), an inverse-time breaker of at most 70 A (28 x 2.5), or a dual-element fuse of 50 A (28 x 1.75 = 49 A, next size up).

A motor feeder's short-circuit and ground-fault device may not be larger than the largest branch-circuit protective device of any motor in the group plus the sum of the FLCs of the other motors; if this is not a standard size, round down.
