Example: for 460 V motors of 27 A (70 A inverse-time breaker), 21 A and 14 A, the feeder breaker may be at most 70 + 21 + 14 = 105 A, so 100 A (next lower standard size).
A motor disconnecting means must have an ampere rating of at least 115% of the motor's full-load current.

A motor disconnect may be a listed motor-circuit switch rated in horsepower, a listed molded-case circuit breaker or molded-case switch, and others; for stationary motors of 2 hp or less at 300 V or less, a general-use switch rated at least twice the motor FLC, or an AC snap switch where FLC is no more than 80% of its rating, may be used.

A disconnect must be within sight of the motor controller, and a disconnect must also be within sight of the motor and driven machinery; the controller disconnect may serve if it is within sight, or (under exceptions) if it is lockable in the open position where a local disconnect is impracticable or more hazardous.
Single-phase motor FLC at 115 V / 230 V: 1/2 hp 9.8/4.9 A; 3/4 hp 13.8/6.9 A; 1 hp 16/8 A; 1-1/2 hp 20/10 A; 2 hp 24/12 A.
Single-phase motor FLC at 115 V / 230 V: 3 hp 34/17 A; 5 hp 56/28 A; 7-1/2 hp 80/40 A; 10 hp 100/50 A. At 208 V: 1 hp 8.8 A; 2 hp 13.2 A; 3 hp 18.7 A; 5 hp 30.8 A.
Three-phase induction motor FLC at 460 V: 1 hp 2.1 A; 2 hp 3.4 A; 3 hp 4.8 A; 5 hp 7.6 A; 7-1/2 hp 11 A; 10 hp 14 A; 15 hp 21 A; 20 hp 27 A.
Three-phase induction motor FLC at 460 V: 25 hp 34 A; 30 hp 40 A; 40 hp 52 A; 50 hp 65 A; 60 hp 77 A; 75 hp 96 A; 100 hp 124 A.
Three-phase induction motor FLC at 230 V: 1 hp 4.2 A; 3 hp 9.6 A; 5 hp 15.2 A; 7-1/2 hp 22 A; 10 hp 28 A; 15 hp 42 A; 20 hp 54 A; 25 hp 68 A; 30 hp 80 A; 40 hp 104 A; 50 hp 130 A.
Three-phase induction motor FLC at 208 V: 5 hp 16.7 A; 7-1/2 hp 24.2 A; 10 hp 30.8 A; 15 hp 46.2 A; 20 hp 59.4 A; 25 hp 74.8 A; 30 hp 88 A.
Motor table voltages are rated motor voltages; the listed currents apply to system voltages of 110-120, 220-240, 440-480 and 550-600 V (for example, use the 460 V column for a 480 V system).
Branch-circuit conductors supplying power conversion equipment (such as a variable-frequency drive) must have an ampacity of at least 125% of the equipment's rated input current.
Branch-circuit conductors for a single motor-compressor must have an ampacity of at least 125% of the rated-load current or the branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater.

Motor-compressor short-circuit and ground-fault protection may not exceed 175% of the rated-load current or branch-circuit selection current; if that will not carry the starting current, it may be increased to 225%.

Multimotor and combination-load AC equipment is marked with a minimum circuit ampacity (MCA) and maximum overcurrent protection (MOCP); conductors are sized from the MCA and the breaker or fuse may not exceed the MOCP.
A disconnect for hermetic refrigerant motor-compressors must have an ampere rating of at least 115% of the rated-load current or branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater.

The AC/refrigeration disconnect must be within sight of and readily accessible from the equipment; it may be mounted on or in the unit but not on panels designed for access or where it covers the nameplate.
A cord-and-plug-connected room air conditioner may not exceed 80% of the branch-circuit rating when it is the only load, or 50% when the circuit also supplies lighting or other appliances.
Flexible cords for room air conditioners may not exceed 10 ft for 120 V units or 6 ft for 208 V or 240 V units.
Single-phase cord-and-plug-connected room air conditioners must have a factory-installed LCDI, AFCI or heat detecting circuit interrupter (HDCI) in the power supply cord.
Conductors from generator terminals to the first overcurrent device must have an ampacity of at least 115% of the generator nameplate current. Example: a 100 A nameplate requires 115 A conductors.

Generators (other than cord-and-plug-connected portable units) need a disconnecting means, lockable in the open position, that disconnects the generator and its protective and control devices from the circuits it supplies.

For one- and two-family dwellings, generators other than cord-and-plug-connected portables need an emergency shutdown device located outside the dwelling at a readily accessible location (added in NEC 2020).

For transformers 1000 V or less with primary-only protection, the primary OCPD may be up to 125% of rated primary current when that current is 9 A or more (next higher standard size permitted), 167% when less than 9 A, and 300% when less than 2 A.

With both primary and secondary protection, the primary OCPD may be up to 250% of rated primary current, and the secondary OCPD up to 125% of rated secondary current (9 A or more; next higher standard size permitted) or 167% (less than 9 A).
Example: a 75 kVA, 3-phase transformer with a 480 V primary draws 75,000 / (480 x 1.732) = 90.2 A; 90.2 x 1.25 = 112.8 A, so the next higher standard size, 125 A, may protect the primary.
Example: the 208Y/120 V secondary of a 75 kVA transformer carries 75,000 / (208 x 1.732) = 208.2 A; 208.2 x 1.25 = 260 A, so the next higher standard size, 300 A, may protect the secondary.

Indoor dry-type transformers rated 112.5 kVA or less must be at least 12 in from combustible material unless separated by a fire-resistant, heat-insulating barrier; those over 112.5 kVA generally must be in a fire-resistant transformer room unless they have Class 155 or higher insulation and are separated by barriers or spacing.

Dry-type transformers of 1000 V or less and not over 50 kVA may be installed in hollow spaces such as above a suspended ceiling, provided they are not permanently closed in and ventilation is adequate.

Transformers other than Class 2 and Class 3 need a disconnecting means located within sight of the transformer, or, if remote, lockable in the open position with its location field-marked on the transformer.
Hazardous location classes: Class I has flammable gases or vapors; Class II has combustible dust; Class III has ignitible fibers or flyings.

Division 1 is where ignitible concentrations exist under normal operating conditions (or often during repair, maintenance or leakage); Division 2 is where they exist only under abnormal conditions such as accidental rupture or ventilation failure, or areas adjacent to Division 1.

The zone system for Class I locations uses Zone 0 (present continuously or for long periods), Zone 1 (likely in normal operation) and Zone 2 (not likely in normal operation and only for short periods); combustible dusts use Zones 20, 21 and 22.
Class I groups: A acetylene; B hydrogen; C ethylene; D propane, gasoline and natural gas. Class II groups: E metal dusts; F carbonaceous dusts such as coal; G grain, flour, wood and plastic dusts.

Permitted Class I, Division 1 wiring methods include threaded RMC or threaded steel IMC, Type MI cable, and (in industrial establishments with restricted access) MC-HL and ITC-HL; PVC or RTRC is allowed underground only when encased in at least 2 in of concrete with at least 24 in of cover.

In Class I, Division 1 locations, a conduit seal is required in each conduit entry into an explosionproof enclosure containing ignition sources (switches, breakers, fuses, relays), located within 18 in of the enclosure.

A conduit leaving a Class I, Division 1 or Division 2 location needs a boundary seal within 10 ft of the boundary on either side, with no union, coupling, box or fitting (except listed reducers) between the seal and the boundary.
Sealing compound in a conduit seal must be at least as thick as the trade size of the sealing fitting, and never less than 5/8 in.
Threaded conduit entries into explosionproof equipment must be made up wrenchtight with at least 5 threads fully engaged (factory-threaded NPT entries on listed equipment: at least 4-1/2 threads).

Branch circuits in patient care spaces need redundant grounding: a metal raceway or cable armor that qualifies as an equipment grounding conductor plus an insulated copper equipment grounding conductor.

Each general care (Category 2) patient bed location needs at least 8 receptacles, and each critical care (Category 1) patient bed location needs at least 14 receptacles, at least one of which is on the normal system or a different critical-branch transfer switch.
facts.note: Counts adopted from NFPA 99 in NEC 2014 and carried forward; confirm with 2023 text.

facts.fact: Receptacles at patient bed locations in general care and critical care spaces must be listed 'hospital grade' and so identified.
A hospital essential electrical system is divided into three branches: life safety, critical and equipment.

A dwelling with a permanently installed pool must have at least one 125 V, 15 A or 20 A receptacle on a general-purpose branch circuit located not less than 6 ft and not more than 20 ft from the inside wall of the pool, and not more than 6-1/2 ft above the floor or grade.

Receptacles for pool pump motors and other loads must be at least 6 ft from the inside walls of the pool; receptacles for the circulation and sanitation system must be grounding type with GFCI protection.
All 15 A and 20 A, 125-250 V receptacles within 20 ft of the inside walls of a pool require GFCI protection.
New outdoor luminaires, lighting outlets and ceiling fans over a pool or within 5 ft horizontally of its inside walls must be at least 12 ft above the maximum water level.

Luminaires and lighting outlets between 5 ft and 10 ft horizontally from the inside walls of a pool need GFCI protection unless installed at least 5 ft above the maximum water level and rigidly attached.
Switching devices must be at least 5 ft horizontally from the inside walls of a pool unless separated by a solid fence, wall or other permanent barrier.
The pool equipotential bonding conductor must be solid copper (insulated, covered or bare) not smaller than 8 AWG.

Perimeter surfaces extending 3 ft horizontally beyond the inside walls of a pool must be bonded; one method is an 8 AWG bare solid copper ring 18 to 24 in from the inside walls, secured 4 to 6 in below the subgrade.
Pool water must have an intentional bond of conductive surfaces totaling at least 9 sq in in contact with the water.

Fixed metal parts within 5 ft horizontally of the inside walls of a pool and less than 12 ft above the maximum water level must be bonded (with exceptions, such as when separated by a permanent barrier).
Outlets supplying pool pump motors on branch circuits rated 150 V or less to ground and 60 A or less, single- or 3-phase, require GFCI protection.

Underground wiring may not be under a pool or within 5 ft horizontally of its inside walls unless necessary to supply pool equipment, in which case RMC or IMC needs at least 6 in of cover and listed nonmetallic raceway for direct burial needs at least 18 in.

Overhead utility insulated cables (0-750 V, supported on a messenger) must clear the pool water level, edge and diving platform base by 22-1/2 ft; other conductors up to 15 kV need 25 ft, and over 15 kV to 50 kV need 27 ft. Clearance above observation stands and diving platforms is 14-1/2 ft, 17 ft and 18 ft respectively.
Communications, radio and TV coaxial cables must be at least 10 ft above pools, diving structures and observation stands.

A maintenance disconnect is required for pool utilization equipment other than lighting; it must be readily accessible, within sight of the equipment, and at least 5 ft horizontally from the inside walls of the pool unless separated by a permanent barrier.

For an indoor spa or hot tub, receptacles must be at least 6 ft from the inside walls; at least one 125 V, 15/20 A receptacle must be between 6 ft and 10 ft away; and 125 V receptacles rated 30 A or less within 10 ft require GFCI.
facts.note: Based on NEC 2017/2020 680.43(A) text; NEC 2023 reorganized GFCI rules into 680.5, so confirm 2023 wording.

facts.fact: Wall switches must be at least 5 ft horizontally from the inside walls of an indoor spa or hot tub.

Spas and hot tubs (other than at single-family dwellings) need a clearly labeled emergency shutoff for the recirculation and jet motors, readily accessible to users, at least 5 ft away, adjacent to and within sight of the spa.
facts.note: Cited from NEC 2020; NEC 2023 reorganized parts of Article 680, so confirm the 2023 section number.

facts.fact: Hydromassage bathtubs must be on an individual branch circuit with a readily accessible GFCI, and all 125 V single-phase receptacles rated 30 A or less within 6 ft horizontally of the tub's inside walls need GFCI protection.
Metal piping and grounded metal parts in contact with the circulating water of a hydromassage tub must be bonded together with a solid copper conductor not smaller than 8 AWG.
Wet-niche and other underwater pool luminaires must be installed with the top of the lens at least 18 in below the normal water level, unless listed for a shallower depth (not less than 4 in).
Fixed or stationary equipment for a permanently installed pool (other than underwater luminaires) may be connected with a flexible cord no longer than 3 ft.
Cord-connected storable pool filter pumps must have GFCI protection built into the attachment plug or in the cord within 12 in of the plug.
Maximum PV system DC voltage is 600 V on or in one- and two-family dwellings and 1000 V on or in other types of buildings.

PV source circuit maximum current is the sum of parallel module short-circuit currents x 125%; conductors and OCPDs are then sized at 125% of that maximum current, a combined 156% of Isc. Example: Isc 10 A x 1.56 = 15.6 A, so a 20 A fuse.

PV rapid shutdown: controlled conductors outside the array boundary (1 ft from the array in all directions) or more than 3 ft inside a building must drop to 30 V or less within 30 seconds of initiation; inside the array boundary, 80 V or less within 30 seconds or a listed PV hazard control system.
New in NEC 2023, PV systems on non-enclosed detached structures such as carports, trellises and shade structures are exempt from rapid shutdown.

The '120% rule': when the PV breaker is at the opposite end of a busbar from the main supply breaker, 125% of the inverter output current plus the main OCPD rating may not exceed 120% of the busbar rating. Example: a 200 A bus with a 200 A main allows 40 A of backfeed, so inverter output may be at most 32 A (40 / 1.25).
Alternatively, 125% of the inverter output current plus the ratings of all overcurrent devices supplying the busbar may not exceed 100% of the busbar ampacity.
A PV system disconnecting means must be at a readily accessible location and permanently marked 'PV SYSTEM DISCONNECT' or equivalent.
Each outlet installed for charging electric vehicles must be supplied by an individual branch circuit with no other outlets (except as permitted for EVSE load management).
Overcurrent protection for EVSE feeders and branch circuits must be rated for continuous duty at no less than 125% of the maximum load of the EVSE. Example: a 48 A charger needs a 60 A breaker.
All receptacles installed for electric vehicle charging must have GFCI protection for personnel.
Emergency systems must deliver power within 10 seconds after the normal supply fails.
Legally required standby systems must deliver power within 60 seconds after the normal supply fails.

Optional standby systems protect property or processes where life safety does not depend on them (such as a home generator); there is no required transfer time, and the user may choose manual or automatic transfer.

Emergency circuit wiring must be kept entirely independent of other wiring (not in the same raceway, cable, box or cabinet), except in transfer equipment, in emergency luminaires supplied by two sources, and certain other listed cases.
Storage batteries and unit equipment for emergency systems must carry the load for at least 1-1/2 hours (90 minutes) without voltage falling below 87.5% of normal.
Generator sets for emergency systems need an on-site fuel supply for at least 2 hours of full-demand operation.
Emergency systems must be witness-tested by the AHJ upon completion, tested periodically on an AHJ-approved schedule, and have written records of tests and maintenance kept.
Overcurrent devices in emergency and legally required standby systems must be selectively coordinated, so only the device nearest a fault opens; coordination must be documented by a qualified person.
Emergency lighting must be arranged so that the failure of any one lighting element (such as a lamp burning out) cannot leave an area that requires emergency illumination in total darkness.

For optional standby, manual transfer requires capacity for all loads to be operated at one time; automatic transfer requires capacity for the full load transferred unless a load management system is used. Transfer equipment must prevent inadvertent interconnection of normal and standby sources.
A sign must be placed at the service entrance indicating the type and location of each on-site optional standby power source.

facts.source: Power formulas (P = I^2 x R; P = E^2 / R)
facts.fact: Power can be found as P = I squared x R or P = E squared / R. Example: 10 A through a 5 ohm resistor is 10 x 10 x 5 = 500 W.
Example: a 1,500 W heater on 120 V draws 1,500 / 120 = 12.5 A, and its resistance is E squared / P = 14,400 / 1,500 = 9.6 ohms.
For a fixed resistance, power varies with the square of voltage: doubling the voltage quadruples the power. Example: the 9.6 ohm heater on 240 V produces 240 x 240 / 9.6 = 6,000 W instead of 1,500 W.
A 4,800 W, 240 V resistive heater run at 208 V produces 4,800 x (208/240) squared = about 3,605 W, roughly 75% of its rating.

In a series circuit, total resistance is the sum of the resistances, the same current flows through every part, and the voltage drops add up to the source voltage. Example: 10, 20 and 30 ohms in series on 120 V = 60 ohms, 2 A, with drops of 20, 40 and 60 V.

In a parallel circuit, every branch has the same voltage, total current is the sum of branch currents, and total resistance is less than the smallest branch. For two resistors, RT = (R1 x R2) / (R1 + R2); 6 ohms and 3 ohms in parallel = 18 / 9 = 2 ohms.
Equal resistors in parallel: total resistance = one resistor's value divided by the number of resistors. Example: four 20 ohm resistors in parallel = 5 ohms.

Single-phase voltage drop: VD = 2 x K x I x L / CM, where K = 12.9 for copper (21.2 for aluminum), I is amps, L is one-way length in feet, and CM is circular mils from Chapter 9 Table 8. Example: 20 A, 100 ft, 12 AWG copper (6,530 cmil): 2 x 12.9 x 20 x 100 / 6,530 = 7.9 V, or 6.6% of 120 V.
Three-phase voltage drop: VD = 1.732 x K x I x L / CM. Example: 50 A, 200 ft, 6 AWG copper (26,240 cmil): 1.732 x 12.9 x 50 x 200 / 26,240 = 8.5 V, about 1.8% of 480 V.

To size a conductor for voltage drop, use CM = 2 x K x I x L / VD. Example: 240 V single-phase, 40 A, 150 ft, 3% (7.2 V): 2 x 12.9 x 40 x 150 / 7.2 = 21,500 cmil, so 6 AWG (26,240 cmil) is needed; 8 AWG (16,510) is too small.
Maximum one-way length for a given voltage drop: L = VD x CM / (2 x K x I). Example: 10 AWG copper (10,380 cmil), 20 A, 120 V at 3% (3.6 V): 3.6 x 10,380 / (2 x 12.9 x 20) = about 72 ft.
Aluminum uses K = 21.2 in the voltage drop formula. Example: 30 A single-phase, 150 ft, 4 AWG aluminum (41,740 cmil): 2 x 21.2 x 30 x 150 / 41,740 = about 4.6 V.

facts.source: Voltage drop by resistance (VD = I x R)
facts.fact: Voltage drop can also be found with Table 8 resistance: R = (2 x one-way length / 1,000) x ohms per 1,000 ft. Example: 12 AWG stranded copper (1.98 ohms/kft), 100 ft one way, 16 A: R = 0.2 x 1.98 = 0.396 ohm; VD = 16 x 0.396 = 6.3 V.
Power factor = true power (watts) / apparent power (volt-amperes). Example: a load drawing 8 kW and 10 kVA has a power factor of 0.8 (80%). For purely resistive loads, watts = VA and PF = 1.
Apparent power, true power and reactive power form a right triangle: kVA squared = kW squared + kVAR squared. Example: 10 kVA at 0.8 PF = 8 kW and 6 kVAR.
Single-phase current I = VA / E; three-phase current I = VA / (E x 1.732). Example: a 45 kVA load at 208 V three-phase draws 45,000 / (208 x 1.732) = about 125 A.
Example: a 25 kVA single-phase transformer with a 240 V secondary has a full-load secondary current of 25,000 / 240 = about 104 A.
Three-phase current from kW: I = W / (E x 1.732 x PF). Example: 100 kW at 480 V and 0.9 PF = 100,000 / (480 x 1.732 x 0.9) = about 134 A.

In an ideal transformer, Vp / Vs = Np / Ns = Is / Ip, so stepping voltage down steps current up by the same ratio. Example: a 480:120 V (4:1) transformer with 10 A on the primary delivers 40 A on the secondary.
Ignoring losses, primary kVA equals secondary kVA in a transformer; only voltage and current change.
In a wye system, line voltage = phase (coil) voltage x 1.732 and line current = phase current. Example: 120 V x 1.732 = 208 V, which gives a 208Y/120 V system.
In a delta system, line voltage = phase (coil) voltage and line current = phase current x 1.732.

In a 120/240 V, 4-wire delta (high-leg) system, the high leg measures about 208 V to the neutral (120 x 1.732), so it may not supply 120 V loads; it is marked orange and placed in the B phase position.
On a 120/240 V single-phase 3-wire circuit, the neutral carries the difference between the two line currents. Example: 30 A on one leg and 20 A on the other leaves 10 A on the neutral.

For unbalanced linear loads on a 3-phase 4-wire wye, neutral current = square root of (A squared + B squared + C squared - AB - BC - CA). Example: 50, 40 and 30 A gives the square root of 300 = 17.3 A. Balanced linear loads produce 0 A on the neutral.
1 horsepower = 746 W, and efficiency = output / input. Example: a 10 hp motor (7,460 W output) at 85% efficiency draws 7,460 / 0.85 = about 8,776 W input.
1 watt = 3.412 BTU per hour, so 1 kW = 3,412 BTU/h.

Conductor resistance increases in direct proportion to length and decreases as cross-sectional area increases; doubling the length doubles the resistance. Each decrease of 6 AWG numbers roughly quadruples the area (14 AWG = 4,110 cmil; 8 AWG = 16,510 cmil).

Inductive reactance XL = 2 x pi x f x L and capacitive reactance XC = 1 / (2 x pi x f x C). In an inductive circuit current lags voltage; in a capacitive circuit current leads voltage ('ELI the ICE man').
Impedance Z = square root of (R squared + (XL - XC) squared), and AC Ohm's law is I = E / Z. Example: R = 30 ohms and XL = 40 ohms gives Z = 50 ohms; at 120 V, I = 2.4 A and PF = R/Z = 0.6.
Kirchhoff's current law: current entering a junction equals current leaving it. Kirchhoff's voltage law: the sum of the voltage drops around a closed loop equals the source voltage.

Batteries in series add voltage at the same amp-hour rating; in parallel they add amp-hour capacity at the same voltage. Example: two 12 V, 100 Ah batteries give 24 V/100 Ah in series or 12 V/200 Ah in parallel.
Capacitors in parallel add directly (CT = C1 + C2); capacitors in series combine like resistors in parallel. Inductors combine like resistors (add in series).
US power is 60 Hz (one cycle every 1/60 s). RMS = 0.707 x peak and peak = 1.414 x RMS, so 120 V RMS is about 170 V peak.
Synchronous speed (RPM) = 120 x frequency / number of poles. At 60 Hz a 2-pole motor runs at 3,600 RPM synchronous and a 4-pole at 1,800 RPM; actual speed is slightly lower due to slip.
The rotation of a three-phase motor is reversed by interchanging any two of the three line leads.
Improving power factor (for example with capacitors on inductive motor loads) reduces the kVA and current needed to deliver the same kW of real power.

On construction sites, all 120 V, single-phase, 15 A and 20 A receptacle outlets that are not part of the building's permanent wiring and are used by employees must have approved GFCI protection, unless the employer uses an assured equipment grounding conductor program.

Receptacles on a two-wire, single-phase portable or vehicle-mounted generator rated 5 kW or less do not need GFCIs if the generator's circuit conductors are insulated from the frame and all other grounded surfaces.
An assured equipment grounding conductor program must have a written description kept at the jobsite and one or more competent persons designated to implement it.

Under an assured grounding program, cord sets, attachment caps, plugs, receptacles and cord-and-plug equipment must be visually inspected before each day's use for external defects such as missing pins or damaged insulation.

Assured grounding program tests: all equipment grounding conductors must be tested for continuity, and each receptacle and attachment plug must be tested for correct attachment of the equipment grounding conductor to its proper terminal.

Assured grounding tests are required before first use, before return to service after repair, after any incident that could have caused damage, and at intervals not exceeding 3 months (6 months for fixed cord sets and receptacles not exposed to damage).

Assured grounding tests must be recorded (logs, color coding or other effective means) showing each item tested, whether it passed and the last test date or interval, and the records kept available at the jobsite.
Temporary electrical power and lighting installations must be removed immediately upon completion of construction or the purpose for which they were installed.
Extension cord sets used with portable electric tools and appliances must be three-wire type and designed for hard or extra-hard usage (such as types S, ST, SO, STO, SJ, SJO, SJT, SJTO).

Flexible cords must be used only in continuous lengths without splice or tap; hard-service cords 12 AWG or larger may be repaired if the splice keeps the insulation, outer sheath and usage characteristics of the original cord.

Lamps for general temporary illumination must be protected from accidental contact or breakage (guards), metal-case sockets must be grounded, and temporary lights may not be suspended by their cords unless designed for it.
Portable lighting used in wet or conductive locations, such as drums, tanks and vessels, must operate at 12 V or less, or 120 V if protected by a GFCI.

On temporary wiring, branch-circuit conductors may not lie on the floor, open conductor runs must be fastened at intervals not exceeding 10 ft, receptacles must be grounding type, and receptacles for other than temporary lighting may not be on branch circuits that supply temporary lighting.
Employees may not work close enough to any part of an electric power circuit to contact it unless the circuit is de-energized and grounded or effectively guarded by insulation or other means.
Worn or frayed electric cords or cables may not be used, and extension cords may not be fastened with staples, hung from nails or suspended by wire.

Controls that are deactivated during work on equipment or circuits must be tagged, and de-energized equipment or circuits must be rendered inoperative with tags attached at all points where they could be energized.

Unqualified persons (and the longest conductive object they handle) must stay at least 10 ft from unguarded energized overhead lines of 50 kV or less, plus 4 in for every 10 kV over 50 kV. Example: a 138 kV line requires 10 ft + 35.2 in, about 12 ft 11 in.

Minimum crane clearance from power lines: up to 50 kV, 10 ft; over 50-200 kV, 15 ft; over 200-350 kV, 20 ft; over 350-500 kV, 25 ft; over 500-750 kV, 35 ft; over 750-1,000 kV, 45 ft. Alternatively the employer may keep 20 ft for lines up to 350 kV and 50 ft for lines over 350 kV up to 1,000 kV.
Approach distances for qualified persons (AC): 300 V and less, avoid contact; over 300 V to 750 V, 1 ft; over 750 V to 2 kV, 1 ft 6 in; over 2 kV to 15 kV, 2 ft; over 15 kV to 37 kV, 3 ft.

When de-energizing for lockout, control devices such as push buttons, selector switches and interlocks may not be the sole means of de-energizing; a qualified person must verify with test equipment that the circuit is de-energized (including checking for induced or backfed voltage).
A lock and tag go on each disconnecting means; a tag alone may be used only when a lock cannot be applied, and then an additional safety measure equivalent to a lock is required.
Energy control (lockout/tagout) procedures must be inspected periodically, at least annually, by an authorized employee other than the ones using the procedure.

Live parts of electric equipment operating at 50 V or more must be guarded against accidental contact by enclosures, by location in a room accessible only to qualified persons, by partitions or screens, or by elevation of 8 ft or more above the floor.
A made electrode (such as a ground rod) on a construction site that measures more than 25 ohms to ground must be supplemented by one additional electrode installed at least 6 ft away.

questions.q: A load where the maximum current is expected to continue for how long is a continuous load?
questions.why: Article 100 defines a continuous load as one lasting 3 hours or more; the other times are not in the definition.

questions.q: 'Within sight' means visible and not more than what distance away?
questions.why: In sight from means visible and not more than 50 ft distant. 25, 75 and 100 ft are not the defined distance.

questions.q: A Class A GFCI must trip when ground-fault current reaches:
questions.why: Class A GFCIs trip at 6 mA or more and must not trip below 4 mA; 30 mA is a typical equipment-protection level, not Class A.

questions.q: In the NEC, which wording indicates a permissive rule?
questions.why: 'Shall be permitted' is permissive. 'Shall' and 'shall not' are mandatory, and informational notes are not enforceable.

questions.q: In NEC 2023, where are nearly all definitions located?
questions.why: NEC 2023 consolidated almost all definitions into Article 100; before that many lived in individual articles' .2 sections.

questions.q: Unless equipment is listed and marked otherwise, terminations on a 60 A circuit using 6 AWG conductors are based on which temperature column?
questions.why: Circuits rated 100 A or less (or marked for 14-1 AWG) use 60 C unless the equipment is listed and marked for 75 C.

questions.q: Minimum working space depth for a 480Y/277 V panelboard with exposed live parts on one side and a concrete wall on the other is:
questions.why: A concrete wall is grounded, so this is Condition 2; at 151-600 V to ground that is 3-1/2 ft. 3 ft is Condition 1 and 4 ft is Condition 3.

questions.q: Working space in front of a panelboard must be at least how wide (or the equipment width, if greater)?
questions.why: Working space width is 30 in or the equipment width, whichever is greater.

questions.q: Equipment rated 1200 A or more and over 6 ft wide requires an entrance to the working space at each end at least how wide?
questions.why: Each entrance must be at least 24 in wide and 6-1/2 ft high.

questions.q: Personnel doors within 25 ft of the working space must have listed panic hardware when the equipment is rated at least:
questions.why: The panic or fire-exit hardware rule applies to equipment rated 800 A or more; 1200 A is the large-equipment two-entrance threshold.

questions.q: The dedicated electrical space above a panelboard extends from the floor to what height above the equipment (or the structural ceiling, if lower)?
questions.why: The dedicated space runs to 6 ft above the equipment or to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower.

questions.q: Under NEC 2023, a permanent arc-flash label is required on service and feeder-supplied equipment (other than dwellings) rated at least:
questions.why: NEC 2023 set the threshold at 1000 A for service and feeder-supplied equipment; NEC 2020 used 1200 A for service equipment only.

questions.q: On a 4-wire delta system, the high leg must be marked with which color?
questions.why: 110.15 requires the higher-voltage-to-ground conductor to be durably marked orange (or by another effective means).

questions.q: What is the maximum cord-and-plug-connected load permitted on a 20 A receptacle supplied by a 20 A branch circuit?
questions.why: Table 210.21(B)(2) limits a 20 A receptacle on a 20 A circuit to 16 A (80%).

questions.q: On a 40 A branch circuit serving more than one receptacle, which receptacle ratings are permitted?
questions.why: Table 210.21(B)(3) allows 40 A or 50 A receptacles on a 40 A circuit.

questions.q: A household range rated 8-3/4 kW or more requires a branch circuit rated at least:
questions.why: Ranges rated 8-3/4 kW or more need a minimum 40 A branch circuit rating.

questions.q: On a 20 A branch circuit that also supplies lighting, fastened-in-place equipment (other than luminaires) may not exceed what percentage of the circuit rating?
questions.why: Fastened-in-place equipment is limited to 50% when lighting or cord-connected equipment is also supplied; 80% is the limit for one cord-and-plug item.

questions.q: Which load is NOT permitted on a new NEC 2023 10 A branch circuit?
c: A bathroom exhaust fan on the lighting circuit
A gas fireplace on an individual circuit
questions.why: 10 A circuits may serve lighting, dwelling exhaust fans on lighting circuits, or a gas fireplace, but not receptacle outlets.

questions.q: A dwelling bathroom receptacle circuit must be rated:
questions.why: At least one 120 V, 20 A branch circuit is required for bathroom receptacles.

questions.q: The NEC informational note recommends a maximum combined feeder plus branch-circuit voltage drop of:
questions.why: The notes suggest 3% on a branch circuit or feeder and 5% total; they are recommendations, not requirements.

questions.q: A multiwire branch circuit must be provided with:
c: Simultaneous disconnection of all ungrounded conductors
A separate neutral for each hot
questions.why: 210.4(B) requires a means (2-pole breaker or handle ties) that disconnects all ungrounded conductors of the MWBC at the same time.

questions.q: Under NEC 2023, what is required at a kitchen island where no receptacle is installed?
questions.why: NEC 2023 made island receptacles optional but requires provisions for future addition; below-counter receptacles are no longer allowed.

questions.q: Under NEC 2020, an island countertop of 27 sq ft requires how many receptacle outlets?
questions.why: One for the first 9 sq ft plus one for each additional 18 sq ft: 9 + 18 = 27 sq ft, so 2.

questions.q: Kitchen countertop receptacles installed above the countertop may be no more than how far above it?
questions.why: Receptacles on or above the countertop must be within 20 in of the surface.

questions.q: A required dwelling bathroom receptacle must be within what distance of the outside edge of each basin?
questions.why: 210.52(D) requires a receptacle within 3 ft of the outside edge of each basin.

questions.q: A dwelling hallway requires at least one receptacle when it is at least how long?
questions.why: Hallways 10 ft or more in length need at least one receptacle.

questions.q: In a dwelling garage, at least one receptacle is required in each vehicle bay at a height of not more than:
questions.why: Each vehicle bay needs a receptacle not more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor.

questions.q: An HVAC service receptacle must be within what distance of the equipment?
questions.why: The receptacle must be within 25 ft of the HVAC equipment, on the same level, and not on the load side of its disconnect.

questions.q: Receptacles are prohibited within a zone extending how far horizontally from the outside edge of a bathtub rim?
questions.why: 406.9(C) prohibits receptacles within 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically of the tub rim or shower threshold.

questions.q: Tamper-resistant receptacles are not required when the receptacle is located more than how far above the floor?
questions.why: Receptacles more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor are exempt from the tamper-resistant requirement.

questions.q: Replacing a 2-prong receptacle with a grounding-type receptacle where no equipment ground exists is permitted if the receptacle is:
c: Protected by an AFCI breaker only
Protected by a GFCI and marked 'No Equipment Ground'
questions.why: A grounding-type replacement must be GFCI protected and marked 'GFCI Protected' and 'No Equipment Ground'. Bonding ground to neutral is never allowed.

questions.q: Outdoor receptacles at a one-family dwelling (front and back) must be no higher than what above grade?
questions.why: The required front and back receptacles must be readily accessible from grade and not more than 6-1/2 ft above grade.

questions.q: Under NEC 2023, which dwelling kitchen receptacles require GFCI protection?
c: Only those within 6 ft of the sink
questions.why: NEC 2020 covered only countertop receptacles; NEC 2023 requires GFCI for all receptacles in dwelling kitchens.

questions.q: Commercial (other than dwelling) GFCI rules cover three-phase receptacles on branch circuits rated 150 V or less to ground and up to:
questions.why: 210.8(B) applies to single-phase circuits up to 50 A and three-phase circuits up to 100 A, both 150 V or less to ground.

questions.q: Under NEC 2023 210.8(D), which appliance branch circuit/outlet requires GFCI protection?
questions.why: NEC 2023 added ranges, wall ovens, cooktops, clothes dryers and microwaves to the specific-appliance GFCI list.

questions.q: In a dwelling, which room is NOT on the 210.12 AFCI list?
questions.why: Dwelling bathrooms are not on the AFCI list (GFCI applies there); bedrooms, laundry areas and hallways are.

questions.q: An existing AFCI-area branch circuit extended by how much, with no new outlets or devices, does not require AFCI protection?
questions.why: Extensions of not more than 6 ft without added outlets or devices (other than splicing devices) are exempt.

questions.q: Dwelling receptacles within what distance of the top inside edge of a sink bowl require GFCI protection?
questions.why: Receptacles within 6 ft of the top inside edge of the sink bowl need GFCI protection.

questions.q: NEC 2023 extended AFCI protection to which new location?
questions.why: NEC 2023 added sleeping quarters in fire, police, ambulance, rescue and ranger stations.

questions.q: Under NEC 2023, the minimum general lighting load for a dwelling unit is:
questions.why: Dwelling general lighting is 3 VA per sq ft (moved to 220.41 in 2023).

questions.q: Under NEC 2023, which area is now included in dwelling floor area for the general lighting load?
c: Unfinished spaces not adaptable for habitable use
questions.why: NEC 2023 removed garages from the exclusions; open porches and unfinished non-adaptable spaces are still excluded.

questions.q: Using Table 220.42(A), the general lighting load for a 20,000 sq ft retail store is:
questions.why: Retail is 1.9 VA/sq ft: 20,000 x 1.9 = 38,000 VA.

questions.q: A dwelling's general lighting, small-appliance and laundry loads total 10,500 VA. What is the demand load per Table 220.45?
In a dwelling load calculation, each small-appliance branch circuit is counted at:
questions.why: 220.52 counts each small-appliance and laundry circuit at 1,500 VA.

questions.q: In a non-dwelling occupancy, each duplex receptacle is calculated at:
questions.why: Each single or multiple receptacle on one yoke is 180 VA.

questions.q: Non-dwelling receptacle loads totaling 30 kVA have a demand load of:
questions.why: First 10 kVA at 100% + remaining 20 kVA at 50% = 20 kVA.

questions.q: Four fastened-in-place appliances in a dwelling total 7,600 VA. The demand load per 220.53 is:
questions.why: Four or more fastened-in-place appliances may be taken at 75%: 7,600 x 0.75 = 5,700 VA.

questions.q: A household clothes dryer with a nameplate of 4,000 W is calculated in the dwelling load at:
questions.why: Dryers are calculated at 5,000 W or the nameplate, whichever is larger.

questions.q: Using Table 220.55 Column C, the demand for one 12 kW household range is:
questions.why: One range not over 12 kW has a Column C demand of 8 kW.

questions.q: What is the Table 220.55 demand load for a single 16 kW range?
questions.why: 16 kW is 4 kW over 12 kW, so increase 8 kW by 4 x 5% = 20%: 9.6 kW.

questions.q: What is the Table 220.54 demand factor for 8 household dryers?
questions.why: Table 220.54 gives 60% for 8 dryers (65% for 7, 55% for 9).

questions.q: Under NEC 2023, the load for electric vehicle supply equipment is calculated at:
c: 5,000 VA or nameplate, whichever is larger
7,200 VA or nameplate, whichever is larger
questions.why: New 220.57 uses 7,200 W (VA) or the EVSE nameplate, whichever is larger.

questions.q: In the dwelling optional method (220.82), general loads are taken at 100% of the first 10 kVA plus what percent of the remainder?
questions.why: 220.82(B) uses 100% of the first 10 kVA and 40% of the remainder.

questions.q: The multifamily optional method demand factor for 10 dwelling units is:
questions.why: Table 220.84 gives 43% for 8-10 units.

questions.q: A feeder neutral carries 300 A of unbalanced load (no nonlinear loads). What neutral load may be used?
Commercial kitchen equipment: what is the Table 220.56 demand factor for 6 or more units?
questions.why: Six or more units use 65%, but never less than the two largest pieces combined.

questions.q: Under NEC 2023, overhead service conductors must have what minimum vertical clearance above a roof (no exceptions applied)?
questions.why: NEC 2023 raised the roof clearance to 8 ft 6 in; NEC 2020 required 8 ft. 3 ft applies only with the 4/12 slope, 300 V exception.

questions.q: Overhead service conductors (300 V or less to ground) over a residential driveway must have a clearance of at least:
questions.why: 12 ft applies over residential property and driveways at 300 V or less to ground; 18 ft is for public streets and truck traffic.

questions.q: Minimum clearance for overhead conductors over a public street is:
questions.why: 18 ft is required over public streets, alleys and roads; 24-1/2 ft is over railroad tracks.

questions.q: The minimum rating of the service disconnect for a one-family dwelling is:
questions.why: 230.79 requires at least a 100 A, 3-wire service disconnect for a one-family dwelling.

questions.q: Under NEC 2023, a service surge-protective device for a dwelling must have a nominal discharge current rating of at least:
questions.why: NEC 2023 added a minimum 10 kA nominal discharge current (In) rating; NEC 2020 had no minimum.

questions.q: The minimum size for underground service conductors is:
questions.why: Service conductors must be at least 8 AWG copper or 6 AWG aluminum/copper-clad aluminum.

questions.q: Service conductors must be kept at least how far from a window that can be opened?
questions.why: 230.9(A) requires 3 ft from windows designed to be opened, doors, porches, balconies, stairs and fire escapes.

questions.q: GFPE is required for solidly grounded wye services over 150 V to ground when the service disconnect is rated at least:
questions.why: Ground-fault protection of equipment applies to service disconnects rated 1000 A or more.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a standard ampere rating for inverse-time circuit breakers?
questions.why: 90, 110 and 175 A are standard ratings; there is no 120 A standard rating (100 A and 110 A precede 125 A).

questions.q: The maximum overcurrent protection for 10 AWG copper (general use, per 240.4(D)) is:
questions.why: 240.4(D) limits 10 AWG copper to 30 A (unless permitted elsewhere, such as motor circuits).

questions.q: A conductor with 380 A ampacity may be protected by which maximum standard overcurrent device under the next-size-up rule?
questions.why: 240.4(B) allows the next higher standard rating (400 A) up to 800 A when conditions are met.

questions.q: Tap conductors under the 25 ft feeder tap rule must have an ampacity of at least what fraction of the feeder overcurrent device rating?
questions.why: 25 ft taps need ampacity of at least 1/3 of the feeder OCPD rating; 1/10 relates to the 10 ft field-installed tap.

questions.q: The center of the grip of a breaker handle in its highest position may be no more than how high above the floor?
questions.why: 240.24(A) and 404.8(A) limit the handle grip height to 6 ft 7 in.

questions.q: Arc energy reduction is required where a breaker's highest continuous current trip setting is at least:
questions.why: 240.87 applies at 1200 A or higher.

questions.q: What is the minimum copper GEC size (Table 250.66) for a service with 3/0 AWG copper service-entrance conductors?
questions.why: 2/0 or 3/0 copper service conductors require a 4 AWG copper GEC.

questions.q: A GEC that is the sole connection to a ground rod need not be larger than:
questions.why: The sole connection to a rod, pipe or plate electrode need not exceed 6 AWG copper (4 AWG aluminum).

questions.q: A GEC that is the sole connection to a concrete-encased electrode need not be larger than:
questions.why: 250.66(B) caps the GEC to a concrete-encased electrode at 4 AWG copper.

questions.q: A concrete-encased electrode must be at least how long?
questions.why: At least 20 ft of 1/2 in rebar or 4 AWG bare copper encased in at least 2 in of concrete.

questions.q: A single ground rod need not be supplemented if its resistance to earth is no more than:
questions.why: A single rod, pipe or plate electrode must be supplemented unless it measures 25 ohms or less.

questions.q: When two ground rods are installed, they must be at least how far apart?
questions.why: Multiple rod, pipe or plate electrodes must be at least 6 ft apart.

questions.q: A ground rod must have at least how much length in contact with the soil?
questions.why: Rods must be at least 8 ft long with at least 8 ft in contact with soil.

questions.q: If rock is encountered, a ground rod may be driven at an angle no greater than how many degrees from vertical?
questions.why: Rods may be angled up to 45 degrees from vertical, or buried in a 30 in deep trench.

questions.q: A ground ring electrode must be buried at least how deep?
questions.why: Ground rings (at least 20 ft of 2 AWG bare copper) are buried at least 30 in.

questions.q: Which may NOT be used as a grounding electrode?
questions.why: Metal underground gas piping is specifically prohibited as a grounding electrode.

questions.q: What is the minimum copper equipment grounding conductor for a circuit protected by a 60 A breaker?
questions.why: Table 250.122 requires 10 AWG copper for overcurrent devices rated up to 60 A.

questions.q: What is the minimum copper equipment grounding conductor for a 200 A feeder?
questions.why: Table 250.122 lists 6 AWG copper (4 AWG aluminum) for 200 A.

questions.q: Service-entrance conductors are four sets of 500 kcmil copper per phase. The main bonding jumper must be at least:
questions.why: Above 1100 kcmil, use 12.5%: 2000 kcmil x 0.125 = 250 kcmil.

questions.q: An 8 AWG copper GEC must be protected by:
c: Nothing if stapled to the wall
RMC, IMC, PVC, RTRC, EMT or cable armor
questions.why: 8 AWG GECs require protection in a raceway or cable armor; 6 AWG and larger may run exposed if not subject to damage.

questions.q: A flexible metal conduit (FMC) run may serve as the equipment grounding conductor only if the circuit is protected at no more than:
questions.why: FMC qualifies only with listed fittings, circuits of 20 A or less, and a total ground-return length of 6 ft or less.

questions.q: The intersystem bonding termination must provide connections for at least how many intersystem bonding conductors?
questions.why: 250.94 requires capacity for at least three intersystem bonding conductors.

questions.q: Interior metal water piping may be used to interconnect grounding electrodes only within what distance of its point of entrance?
questions.why: Only the first 5 ft of interior water pipe from the point of entrance may be used as the interconnecting conductor.

questions.q: Holes bored in wood studs for NM cable must keep the edge of the hole at least how far from the nearest edge of the stud, unless a steel plate is used?
questions.why: 300.4(A)(1) requires 1-1/4 in, or a steel plate at least 1/16 in thick.

questions.q: Minimum cover for direct-burial UF cable in a general location (not under a driveway) is:
questions.why: Direct-burial cables need 24 in of cover in locations not otherwise listed.

questions.q: Minimum cover for rigid metal conduit in a general location is:
questions.why: RMC and IMC require 6 in of cover in general locations.

questions.q: Minimum cover for PVC conduit listed for direct burial (no concrete) in a yard is:
questions.why: Nonmetallic raceway listed for direct burial without concrete encasement needs 18 in.

questions.q: A 120 V, 20 A GFCI-protected residential branch circuit may be buried with a minimum cover of:
questions.why: Residential branch circuits of 120 V or less with GFCI and 20 A maximum OCPD need 12 in.

questions.q: Direct-buried conductors emerging from grade must be protected up to what height above finished grade?
questions.why: Protection is required from the cover depth to at least 8 ft above finished grade.

questions.q: At least how much free conductor must be left at each outlet box for splices or device connections?
questions.why: 300.14 requires at least 6 in of free conductor, with 3 in extending outside small box openings.

questions.q: What is the 75 C ampacity of 3/0 AWG copper in Table 310.16?
What is the 75 C ampacity of 4/0 AWG aluminum in Table 310.16?
questions.why: 4/0 aluminum is 180 A at 75 C; 230 A is 4/0 copper at 75 C.

questions.q: What is the 60 C ampacity of 6 AWG copper in Table 310.16?
questions.why: 6 AWG copper is 55/65/75 A at 60/75/90 C.

questions.q: What adjustment factor applies to 7 to 9 current-carrying conductors in one raceway?
questions.why: 4-6 conductors 80%, 7-9 conductors 70%, 10-20 conductors 50%.

questions.q: What is the temperature correction factor for a 90 C conductor in a 104 F (40 C) ambient?
questions.why: For 36-40 C the factors are 0.82 (60 C), 0.88 (75 C) and 0.91 (90 C).

questions.q: Adjustment factors for more than three current-carrying conductors do not apply to a raceway no longer than:
questions.why: Raceways (nipples) 24 in or less are exempt from bundling adjustment.

questions.q: Using the 83% rule, which minimum copper conductor (75 C) may serve a 200 A single-phase dwelling service with no derating?
questions.why: 200 A x 0.83 = 166 A; 2/0 copper is rated 175 A at 75 C, while 1/0 (150 A) is too small.

questions.q: Conductors may be run in parallel only in sizes of:
questions.why: Parallel conductors must be 1/0 AWG or larger, same length, material, size and insulation.

questions.q: For box fill, a single receptacle on one yoke counts as how many volume allowances?
questions.why: Each yoke or strap counts as two volume allowances based on the largest conductor connected to it.

questions.q: In box fill calculations, all equipment grounding conductors together count as:
questions.why: All EGCs together count as a single volume allowance based on the largest EGC.

questions.q: What is the volume allowance per 6 AWG conductor in a box?
questions.why: Table 314.16(B) lists 5.00 cu in for 6 AWG and 3.00 cu in for 8 AWG.

questions.q: What is the volume of a standard 4 x 2-1/8 in square metal box?
questions.why: A 4 x 2-1/8 in square box is 30.3 cu in; 21.0 is 4 x 1-1/2 square and 42.0 is 4-11/16 x 2-1/8.

questions.q: A straight-pull box for 3 in conduits containing 4 AWG and larger conductors must be at least how long?
questions.why: Straight pulls require 8 times the largest trade size: 8 x 3 = 24 in.

questions.q: A ceiling outlet box for a luminaire must be able to support at least:
questions.why: Ceiling luminaire boxes must support at least 50 lb; heavier luminaires need independent support unless the box is listed for the weight.

questions.q: Boxes listed as the sole support of a ceiling fan may support fans up to:
questions.why: Fan-rated boxes may support up to 70 lb; boxes for fans over 35 lb must be marked with the weight.

questions.q: In a gypsum or plaster wall, a flush box may be set back no more than:
questions.why: In noncombustible surfaces boxes may be set back up to 1/4 in; in combustible surfaces they must be flush or project.

questions.q: NM cable must be secured within how far of every box?
questions.why: NM cable is secured within 12 in of every box and at intervals not exceeding 4-1/2 ft.

questions.q: NM cable must be secured at intervals not exceeding:
questions.why: 334.30 requires securing at intervals not exceeding 4-1/2 ft.

questions.q: EMT must be supported at intervals not exceeding:
questions.why: EMT is supported every 10 ft and within 3 ft of each box or termination.

questions.q: The maximum total bends between pull points in an EMT run is:
questions.why: No more than the equivalent of four quarter bends (360 degrees) between pull points.

questions.q: Type MC cable (four or fewer conductors, 10 AWG or smaller) must be supported at intervals not exceeding:
questions.why: MC cable is supported every 6 ft and secured within 12 in of boxes for small cables.

questions.q: 1 in PVC conduit must be supported at intervals not exceeding:
questions.why: PVC 1/2 through 1 in trade size is supported every 3 ft.

questions.q: PVC conduit requires an expansion fitting where the expected length change is at least:
questions.why: Expansion fittings are required for expected movement of 1/4 in or more.

questions.q: The ampacity of NM cable is based on which conductor temperature rating?
questions.why: NM cable ampacity is limited to the 60 C rating even though conductors are 90 C rated.

questions.q: Flexible metal conduit must be secured within how far of each box?
questions.why: FMC and LFMC are secured within 12 in of each box and every 4-1/2 ft.

questions.q: What is the maximum fill for a conduit with three or more conductors?
questions.why: Over two conductors: 40%. One conductor 53%, two conductors 31%; 60% is for nipples.

questions.q: A conduit nipple 24 in or shorter may be filled to:
questions.why: Nipples 24 in or less may be filled to 60%.

questions.q: How many 12 AWG THHN conductors are permitted in 3/4 in EMT?
questions.why: 0.213 sq in / 0.0133 sq in = 16. Nine is for 1/2 in EMT; 22 is for 14 AWG in 3/4 in EMT.

questions.q: What is the approximate area of one 10 AWG THHN conductor (Table 5)?
questions.why: 10 AWG THHN is 0.0211 sq in; 0.0133 is 12 AWG and 0.0366 is 8 AWG.

questions.q: What is the circular-mil area of 12 AWG copper (Table 8)?
A surface-mounted LED luminaire with a completely enclosed light source in a clothes closet must be at least how far from the storage space?
questions.why: Surface incandescent or LED with an enclosed source needs 12 in; surface fluorescent and recessed types need 6 in.

questions.q: A cord-connected built-in dishwasher's cord must be:
questions.why: Dishwasher and trash compactor cords are 3 to 4 ft; disposer and range hood cords are 18 to 36 in.

questions.q: What is the minimum standard branch-circuit rating for a 4,500 W, 240 V storage water heater (120 gal or less)?
questions.why: It is a continuous load: 18.75 A x 1.25 = 23.4 A, so the minimum standard rating is 25 A; 20 A is too small.

questions.q: An AC general-use snap switch controlling a motor load may be loaded to what percent of its ampere rating?
questions.why: Motor loads on general-use snap switches are limited to 80% of the switch ampere rating.

questions.q: Resistance heating elements in appliances rated over 48 A must be subdivided, with each load protected at not more than:
questions.why: Subdivided loads may not exceed 48 A and are protected at no more than 60 A.

questions.q: Pendants and ceiling fans may not be located within what horizontal distance of a bathtub rim (within 8 ft vertically)?
questions.why: The tub/shower zone is 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the rim or threshold.

questions.q: Branch-circuit conductors for a single continuous-duty motor must be sized at what percent of the motor FLC?
questions.why: 430.22 requires 125% of the table full-load current.

questions.q: Motor branch-circuit conductor ampacity is based on:
questions.why: Conductors and SCGF protection use table FLC; overloads use the nameplate.

questions.q: Maximum inverse-time breaker size (before exceptions) for a motor is what percent of FLC?
questions.why: Inverse-time breakers 250%; dual-element fuses 175%; nontime-delay fuses 300%; instantaneous trip 800%.

questions.q: A motor with a 1.15 service factor has a nameplate FLA of 20 A. The maximum basic overload setting is:
questions.why: Service factor 1.15 or more allows 125%: 20 x 1.25 = 25 A. 23 A (115%) applies to other motors.

questions.q: What is the table full-load current of a 10 hp, 460 V, three-phase motor?
questions.why: Table 430.250 lists 14 A at 460 V; 28 A is the 230 V value.

questions.q: What is the table full-load current of a 1 hp, 115 V, single-phase motor?
questions.why: Table 430.248 lists 16 A at 115 V (8 A at 230 V).

questions.q: Three 460 V motors draw 14 A, 21 A and 27 A. Minimum feeder conductor ampacity is:
A motor disconnect must be rated at least what percent of the motor FLC?
questions.why: Motor disconnects must be rated at least 115% of full-load current.

questions.q: A hermetic motor-compressor's SCGF protection normally may not exceed what percent of rated-load current?
questions.why: 175% is the basic limit; 225% is allowed only if needed for starting.

questions.q: A 120 V room air conditioner's cord may be no longer than:
questions.why: 120 V room AC cords are limited to 10 ft; 208/240 V units to 6 ft.

questions.q: Conductors from generator terminals to the first overcurrent device must have an ampacity of at least what percent of nameplate current?
questions.why: 445.13 requires at least 115% of the generator nameplate current.

questions.q: A transformer (1000 V or less) with primary-only protection and 90 A rated primary current may have a primary OCPD of at most:
questions.why: 125% x 90 A = 112.5 A; the next higher standard size, 125 A, is permitted.

questions.q: Indoor dry-type transformers 112.5 kVA or less must be separated from combustible material by at least:
questions.why: 450.21(A) requires 12 in unless a fire-resistant, heat-insulating barrier is used.

questions.q: Gasoline vapors are classified in which Class I group?
questions.why: Gasoline, propane and natural gas are Group D; acetylene A, hydrogen B, ethylene C.

questions.q: In a Class I, Division 1 location, a conduit seal must be within what distance of an explosionproof enclosure containing ignition sources?
questions.why: Seals must be within 18 in of the enclosure; 10 ft is for boundary seals.

questions.q: Combustible dust locations are which class?
questions.why: Class II is combustible dust; Class I is gases/vapors; Class III is fibers/flyings.

questions.q: How many receptacles are required at each critical care (Category 1) patient bed location?
questions.why: Critical care bed locations need at least 14 receptacles; general care needs 8.

questions.q: The pool equipotential bonding conductor must be at least:
questions.why: 680.26(B) requires solid copper not smaller than 8 AWG.

questions.q: Pool perimeter surfaces must be bonded for what distance beyond the inside walls of the pool?
questions.why: Perimeter surfaces extending 3 ft horizontally beyond the inside walls must be bonded.

questions.q: All 15 A and 20 A, 125-250 V receptacles within what distance of a pool's inside walls require GFCI protection?
questions.why: GFCI is required for these receptacles within 20 ft of the pool.

questions.q: New outdoor luminaires within 5 ft horizontally of a pool must be at least how high above the maximum water level?
questions.why: 680.22(B)(1) requires at least 12 ft above the maximum water level.

questions.q: Pool water must be bonded with conductive surfaces totaling at least:
questions.why: An intentional bond of at least 9 sq in in contact with the pool water is required.

questions.q: Maximum PV system DC voltage on a one-family dwelling is:
questions.why: One- and two-family dwellings are limited to 600 V DC; other buildings to 1000 V.

questions.q: Outside the array boundary, PV rapid shutdown must reduce controlled conductors to no more than:
questions.why: Outside the boundary: 30 V within 30 s; inside: 80 V within 30 s.

questions.q: Emergency systems must provide power within how many seconds of normal power failure?
questions.why: Emergency systems: 10 s. Legally required standby: 60 s.

questions.q: Legally required standby systems must provide power within:
questions.why: 701.12 allows up to 60 seconds; 10 seconds applies to emergency systems.

questions.q: Emergency battery systems and unit equipment must carry the load for at least:
questions.why: Batteries must supply the load for 1-1/2 hours (90 minutes) without dropping below 87.5% of voltage.

questions.q: Overcurrent protection for an EV charger branch circuit must be rated at least what percent of the EVSE maximum load?
questions.why: EVSE is a continuous load; OCPD is at least 125% of maximum load.

questions.q: What is the voltage drop on a 120 V, 20 A single-phase circuit 100 ft one way using 12 AWG copper (K = 12.9, 6,530 cmil)?
What is the total resistance of a 6 ohm and a 3 ohm resistor in parallel?
questions.why: (6 x 3) / (6 + 3) = 18 / 9 = 2 ohms; parallel total is less than the smallest branch.

questions.q: A load uses 8 kW and 10 kVA. What is its power factor?
A 45 kVA balanced load at 208 V three-phase draws about:
questions.why: 45,000 / (208 x 1.732) = about 125 A; 216 A would be single-phase math.

questions.q: A 480:120 V transformer has 10 A on the primary. What is the secondary current?
questions.why: A 4:1 step-down multiplies current by 4: 10 A x 4 = 40 A.

questions.q: On a 120/240 V single-phase circuit, one leg carries 30 A and the other 20 A. Neutral current is:
questions.why: The neutral carries the difference: 30 - 20 = 10 A.

questions.q: In a 120/240 V high-leg delta system, the high leg measures about what voltage to neutral?
questions.why: 120 V x 1.732 = about 208 V, so it cannot serve 120 V loads.

questions.q: What is the synchronous speed of a 4-pole, 60 Hz motor?
On a construction site, OSHA requires GFCI protection (or an assured grounding program) for which temporary receptacles?
questions.why: 1926.404(b)(1) covers 120 V, single-phase 15 and 20 A receptacles not part of permanent wiring.

questions.q: Under an assured equipment grounding conductor program, routine tests are required at intervals not exceeding:
questions.why: Tests are required every 3 months (6 months for fixed cords and receptacles not exposed to damage).

questions.q: Hard-service flexible cords may be spliced/repaired only if they are at least:
questions.why: Only hard-service cords 12 AWG or larger may be repaired, and the splice must keep the cord's properties.

questions.q: An unqualified worker must stay at least how far from an energized overhead line of 50 kV or less?
questions.why: 10 ft for 50 kV or less, plus 4 in per 10 kV above 50 kV.

questions.q: Portable lighting used inside a metal tank must operate at 12 V or less unless it is:
questions.why: 120 V lights may be used in wet/conductive locations only when GFCI protected.

questions.q: OSHA requires lockout/tagout energy control procedures to be inspected at least:
questions.why: Periodic inspections of energy control procedures are required at least annually.
